studies.title: A Sign That Would End It
studies.meaning: Three openings in four lines. Letters that stand alone and are not explained; a book called clarifying; and then, abruptly, an address to the messenger about his own state. He is described as close to killing himself over people who will not believe, which is grief and not anger. The answer is not consolation. It is a statement of what God could do and is not doing: send something from the sky that would bend every neck. Belief is being left at the point where it can still be refused.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the middle period, when the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) had been preaching for years to a city that would not move. The commentators read the third ayah as describing genuine distress rather than a figure of speech, and note that a nearly identical line appears in another Meccan surah. No specific occasion is reported. The surah then turns immediately to seven earlier messengers who faced the same refusal.

keyTerms.note: A participle for slaughtering an animal by cutting right through to the spinal marrow. It names complete destruction, not sadness, and the Quran uses it twice, both times of the same grief.
A word for a neck lowered under a yoke or a hand. It occurs once in the Quran, describing a submission that would be produced by force rather than chosen, which is why it stays hypothetical.
An active participle, so the book does not merely appear clear; it makes other things clear. The form points outward at what is explained rather than inward at the text's own style.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca was a small place. A man who had spent a decade calling his own relatives, his neighbours and the men he traded with, and had been answered with ridicule, met those same people every day at the well and in the assembly. There was no crowd to disappear into and no other city to try. The grief this ayah names was the grief of someone who knew each person who had refused him by name.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for bent necks occurs once in the whole Quran, and the participle for self-destroying grief occurs twice, both times about the same thing. The three letters that open this surah open only one other, and the two are separated by a surah that begins with two of the same letters. None of the openings is explained anywhere in the text.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The fourth line concedes that compulsion is available and rules it out by not using it. That places a limit on what revelation is for: it is not an instrument for producing belief but an offer that has to be able to fail. The third line is stranger. It records that the failure hurt, and that the hurt was not corrected but simply named, which makes grief over other people a thing prophecy contains rather than a flaw in it.

crossReferences.why: Uses almost the identical sentence about grief for people who will not believe a report.
States plainly that God could have made everyone on earth believe, and asks whether people can be compelled.
Says there is no compulsion in religion, which is the settled form of what is left open here.

studies.applyIt: Think of the person whose choices you are carrying: a child, a sibling, a friend who is not listening. Say the thing you have been saying once, plainly, and then stop. Not permanently, just for a week. This passage puts grief over someone else's refusal in the mouth of a prophet, and then declines to remove the refusal. Try holding both.

studies.title: Every Noble Kind In Pairs
studies.meaning: A habit is described rather than an event: no fresh reminder arrives without their turning from it. The word for the reminder means newly given, which the commentators take as newly revealed rather than newly invented. Then the sentence stops arguing and points at the ground. How many noble kinds have been made to grow there, each in pairs. The shift is deliberate. An argument about a message is dropped and a question about vegetation is put in its place.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah opens by naming the pattern it will then illustrate seven times over: a message arrives, and it is turned away from. The reminder is attributed to the Merciful, the name Mecca contested most sharply. No occasion is reported for these ayat. The threat in the second line is left unspecified, and the commentators note that unspecified warnings are characteristic of the Meccan material.

keyTerms.note: A passive participle meaning brought about anew. It describes the reminder as arriving in instalments, each one recent, and it occurs in only one other ayah of the Quran.

The word covers one of a pair and the pair together, which is why translations divide between kinds and pairs. Applied to plants the commentators read it as species, each kind distinct from the others and reproducing as itself.
The word used of a generous host and a well-born man, applied here to plants. It carries usefulness and worth together, so a noble growth is one that gives freely of what it has.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca grew nothing. The valley was stone and the city lived on trade and on food carried in, which made cultivated land something Meccans saw at the other end of a journey and priced accordingly. Dates came from oases days away, grain from the north. To be asked to look at the earth and count the kinds growing in it was, for this audience, to be asked about somebody else's ground and their own dependence on it.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing the reminder as newly given occurs in only one other ayah of the Quran, where it is used in the same complaint about people turning away. The line about the earth is followed by two sentences that then repeat, unchanged, seven more times in this surah, once at the close of each prophet's story.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two claims sit together. Revelation is described as continuous rather than finished, arriving in fresh instalments, which makes turning away a repeated decision instead of a single verdict. And the argument then leaves language behind entirely. A growing thing is offered as evidence, which relocates the case from what a person is told to what a person can walk out and look at. Refusal after that is a refusal of the ground as much as of the message.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for a reminder newly given, in the same report of people turning away.
Draws the same argument from grain and paired growth, ending on pairs people do not know.
Names pairs of fruit growing from one water on one land, and calls the difference a sign.

studies.applyIt: Go and look at one growing thing today with more attention than it deserves. A weed in a pavement crack, the herb dying on your windowsill, a street tree. Sixty seconds. Notice that it is a specific kind and not a general green. This passage answers an argument by pointing at the ground, and the pointing only works if somebody looks.

studies.title: I Fear They Will Deny Me
studies.meaning: The refrain arrives for the first time and will return seven more times: a sign is in this, and most of them did not believe; and your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful. Then the surah begins its long sequence without preamble. God calls Moses and tells him to go to a wrongdoing people, naming them only in the following line. Moses answers with fear, not with objection, and the first thing he says is that he expects to be called a liar.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Moses account in this surah is the longest of the seven and is told almost entirely in dialogue, which the commentators connect to the surah's purpose: a man in Mecca facing a hostile city is being shown a man who faced a king. The story begins at the call, skipping the birth, the river and the years in Midian that other surahs supply. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: A call made across a distance, loud enough to carry. The verb places the caller apart from the one called, which is how the encounter is described throughout: a voice, and no form given.

A question put by God about Pharaoh's people, using the verb for guarding oneself against harm. Phrasing the mission as a question rather than a verdict leaves their situation open at the moment Moses is sent.
Two names that pull in different directions, power and tenderness, held in one phrase. The pairing closes each of the eight sections in this surah, so every account of destruction ends on mercy.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Being called a liar was not an insult in that society; it was a legal position. A man's word was the instrument by which sales, debts, marriages and killings were established, so being publicly held a liar removed him from ordinary dealings. When the Quraysh answered the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) with that charge, they were not describing his character. They were putting him outside the system by which anything could be settled.
studies.didYouKnow: The second sentence of the refrain here occurs eight times in the Quran, and all eight are in this surah, closing the opening and then each of the seven prophet accounts. It is the surah's spine. The Quran contains other repeated refrains, but this one is built to mark the seams of a sequence rather than to punctuate a list.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A prophet is shown afraid before he is shown obedient, and the fear is not rebuked in this line. That establishes something about what being sent involves: the capacity is supplied, the temperament is not replaced. And the errand itself is put as a question about whether the people will be wary, which keeps the outcome open at the moment of sending. Nobody is described as already condemned when the messenger sets out.

crossReferences.why: Tells the same call at greater length, with the fire, the staff and the hand.
Gives the same commission with Moses' fear and the granting of Aaron in reply.
Compresses the whole errand into three short lines addressed directly to Pharaoh.

studies.applyIt: Say out loud the thing you are afraid will happen if you do the difficult task in front of you. Not the task, the fear. That they will laugh, that you will freeze, that it will not work. Moses names his fear first and is sent anyway. Naming it does not remove it; it just stops it from operating unexamined.

studies.title: We Are With You, Listening
studies.meaning: Moses lists three obstacles and asks for one thing. His chest tightens, his tongue will not run free, and there is a killing on his record in Egypt that could cost him his life. He does not ask for these to be removed. He asks for his brother. The answer is a single word of refusal to the fear, then an instruction to go, and then the assurance: We are with you both, listening. Nothing is fixed. Company is given instead.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The killing Moses refers to is the one recounted at length in another surah, where he strikes an Egyptian who was beating a man of his own people and then flees. Here it is compressed to a phrase, on the assumption that the audience knows it. The commentators note that the reply does not deny the danger; it supplies a companion and a promise of presence and sends them anyway.

keyTerms.note: The Arabic for distress is physical: the chest narrowing. Moses reports a symptom rather than an emotion, which is how the Quran usually describes being overwhelmed.
A particle of flat refusal, used to shut down what was just said. Here it answers the fear rather than the request, so the brother is granted and the worry is simply refused.
Singular, although two men are speaking. The classical commentators explain that the word can name a message or an errand borne jointly, so one word covers both of them without error.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Speaking to power in that world was a performance skill. An envoy stood in a court, held a room of hostile men and delivered his message without stumbling, and a man who could not get his words out was finished before he started. Delegations chose their speaker carefully for exactly this reason. Moses asking for a brother who could speak was asking for the standard equipment of anyone sent to a king.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for messenger in the last line of this passage is singular, though two men are told to say it. Arabic grammarians and commentators have discussed the form since the earliest period, reading it either as a noun that can stand for a message or as a form that covers one and many alike. The Quran keeps the singular and does not explain it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: What is given is not competence but company. The stammer stays, the danger stays, the past stays; what changes is that two go instead of one and that the sending includes a claim of presence. The promise is phrased as listening rather than watching, which puts God inside the conversation about to happen rather than above it. Support is described as attention here, and attention is what the frightened person actually lacks.

crossReferences.why: Records the same request as a prayer, asking for an opened chest and an untied tongue.
Grants Aaron as a support and promises that they will not be reached.
Uses the same assurance of presence to a frightened companion in a cave.

studies.applyIt: Ask one person to come with you to the thing you are dreading. The appointment, the difficult conversation, the first session. Not to speak for you, just to be in the room. Moses is not given fluency or safety; he is given his brother. Sending the message and asking someone to stand beside you are two separate acts, and the second is available today.

studies.title: I Did It Then
studies.meaning: Pharaoh does not answer the demand. He answers the man, reaching back to a childhood in his own household and a killing that followed it. The move is to make the messenger's biography the subject. What is remarkable is the reply. Moses does not deny it, explain it or plead the circumstances. He says he did it and that he was among those who had lost their way, and then goes straight on to the next thing without defending himself.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The upbringing Pharaoh cites is the one told in full elsewhere, where the infant is drawn from the river and raised in the palace of the man who had ordered the killing of boys. The killing Moses admits is likewise given at length in another surah. Here both are reduced to a taunt and an answer, and the commentators note that the surah assumes the audience already has the story.

keyTerms.note: The verb for bringing a child up, which the commentators connect with the word for Lord. Pharaoh uses the language of lordship over Moses in the sentence right after Moses names the Lord of the worlds.
A noun form naming a single occurrence of an action. Pharaoh does not name the killing; he uses a word that points at it, which is how an accusation is made without stating the charge.

keyTerms.gloss: those who have lost the way
keyTerms.note: The word for a traveller off the road or a camel gone missing. It admits error without admitting malice, and the commentators read it as ignorance of what would follow rather than a confession of murder.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Bringing up a child not your own created a debt in Arabian society that lasted a lifetime. A foster relationship was a real relationship, counted alongside blood, and reminding a man that you had fed and housed him was a recognised way of asserting a claim over him in public. Pharaoh's opening is therefore not sentimental. It is a legal move, made in front of a court, and everyone listening in Mecca knew the manoeuvre.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb Pharaoh uses for having raised Moses is built from the root the commentators connect with the word for Lord, which Moses had used of God two lines earlier. The exchange therefore sets one claim of lordship against another in the same vocabulary. Neither speaker remarks on it, and the Arabic makes the collision audible without a word of comment.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A prophet is shown admitting a wrong without losing his standing to speak. The admission is placed in the middle of the mission, in front of the person it most damages him with, and the surah does not treat it as a disqualification. That separates the authority of a message from the record of the person carrying it. It also models an answer to accusation that concedes the fact and refuses the inference drawn from it.

crossReferences.why: Gives the killing in full, with Moses' immediate regret and his flight from the city.
Tells how the child came to be raised in the household Pharaoh is now invoking.
Continues the same confrontation, with Pharaoh questioning and Moses answering about earlier generations.

studies.applyIt: The next time someone brings up something you did, try answering in one sentence without the explanation attached. Yes, I did that. Then stop, and let the silence be theirs. The explanation can come later if it is wanted. Most of the energy in these exchanges goes into the defence, and Moses spends none of it.

studies.title: A Favour You Count Against Me
studies.meaning: Moses finishes the admission and turns the account around. He fled, he was given judgement, he was made a messenger; the sequence answers the taunt about his past by not disputing it. Then the sentence that changes the subject of the trial. Is this the favour you hold over me, that you enslaved the Children of Israel? A childhood in the palace is set against a nation in bondage, and the private debt is cancelled by the public one. Pharaoh's reply avoids all of it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Israelites in Egypt are described in the Quran as held in servitude and subjected to the killing of their sons, and this line is the surah's only direct statement of the charge. Reports about the period vary in the Israelite traditions the early commentators sometimes cite, and those are not part of the Quranic account. Pharaoh's counter-question then opens the next exchange. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: The capacity to decide rightly between things, given as a gift before prophethood is mentioned. The commentators read it as understanding and right judgement rather than as legal authority.
To give something and then keep raising it. The verb names a favour turned into leverage, which is why the Quran elsewhere warns against following charity with it.
An intensive verb built from the word for a servant, meaning to reduce people to that condition. This form occurs nowhere else in the Quran, and it names an action rather than a state.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Slavery was ordinary in Mecca and its moral weight was not. Men owned people, and some of the earliest Muslims were among the owned, tortured in the open by masters who faced no consequence. A community hearing this exchange contained both sides of it. Setting a favour done to one man against the bondage of a whole people was, in that city, an argument aimed at people who could do the arithmetic themselves.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb naming what Pharaoh did to the Israelites occurs in this form nowhere else in the Quran. Pharaoh's answer in the third line is a question about what the Lord of the worlds even is, which has the same shape as the objection the previous surah reports being made in Mecca about the name of the Merciful.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A private kindness is weighed against a public wrong and found not to cancel it. That is a claim about how obligation works: personal generosity does not buy immunity from what you have done at scale, and the beneficiary is not silenced by having benefited. The passage also puts the accusation in the mouth of the accused, which is where it carries least advantage and most force. Justice is argued from inside the debt.

crossReferences.why: Warns against cancelling charity by holding it over the person who received it, the move named here.
Describes the same oppression of the Children of Israel and the promise made to them.
Continues the confrontation, with the same charge and the promise of inheritance to come.

studies.applyIt: Think of a favour you have done that you have mentioned more than once. Then decide not to mention it again, starting now. If it was given, it is gone. This exchange shows what a favour becomes once it is used as leverage, and the person on the other side of yours can almost certainly count the times.

studies.title: Lord Of All Between Them
studies.meaning: Pharaoh asks what the Lord of the worlds is, and Moses does not define. He describes a scope: the heavens, the earth, everything between them. The answer is a boundary, not a portrait. Pharaoh turns to the room instead of replying, inviting the court to hear how absurd it sounded, and Moses simply extends the scope backwards to their own ancestors. Then comes the label that ends every serious conversation. This messenger of yours is possessed.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Egyptian court had gods with names, functions and temples, so a question about which one this was had a normal answer, and Moses declines to give one of that kind. Meanwhile the Quraysh were answering the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) with the same word Pharaoh uses at the end here, saying he was possessed. The surah puts an old confrontation and a present one in the same vocabulary. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: From a root for knowledge that has settled beyond doubt. Moses attaches his answer to a condition, so the description only reaches people already willing to be convinced by it.
Pharaoh speaks past Moses to the men around him. The verb is for listening attentively, and the question invites the court to treat an answer as a performance rather than a claim.

Literally covered or affected by unseen beings, the standard Arabian explanation for speech that did not fit. It was also the charge the Quraysh brought, so the word arrives in the surah already loaded.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Calling a man possessed was not name-calling in Arabia; it was a diagnosis with social consequences. The poet and the soothsayer were both understood to be in contact with unseen beings, and that contact explained speech that ordinary men could not produce. The charge therefore did two things at once: it accounted for the eloquence and it removed the speaker's responsibility for it. You did not argue with someone possessed. You made allowances.
studies.didYouKnow: Moses speaks three times in this exchange and widens the frame each time: the heavens and the earth, then their fathers, then the east and the west in the next ayah. He never names a god or gives an attribute. Pharaoh never answers the answer; he changes audience once and then changes subject to the speaker's sanity.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God is answered for by extent rather than by identity. Every reply names a span and refuses a portrait, which keeps the description from becoming one item in a list of gods. That is the point of the exchange: Pharaoh's question assumes a pantheon and expects a slot to be filled, and the answer will not fill one. What cannot be located among other things also cannot be compared with them, and comparison is what the question was for.

crossReferences.why: Continues the same answer, widening it a third time to the east and the west.
Says every messenger before was met with the words sorcerer or possessed, the charge made here.
Denies that anything is like Him, which is the principle behind refusing to name a comparison.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you handle a difficult claim by describing the person who made it. He is angry, she is naive, they are obsessed. It is quick and it feels like analysis. Try answering the claim instead, once, out loud or on paper. Pharaoh's move is available to everyone, and it works by ending the conversation without appearing to.

studies.title: Even If I Bring You Proof
studies.meaning: Moses widens the answer once more, this time along the horizon, and adds a second condition: if you would use your minds. Pharaoh drops argument entirely and reaches for the cell. The threat is precise about method, that Moses will be made one of the imprisoned, which the commentators note was a worse fate in Egypt than the word suggests. Moses answers a threat with an offer. Even if I bring you something plain? And Pharaoh, who has just refused to reason, agrees to look.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Imprisonment in the ancient world was not a sentence served but a disappearance: a man was put somewhere and not heard of again. The commentators describe the Egyptian threat in those terms, which is why Moses treats it as a threat to his life rather than to his liberty. The exchange stands at the hinge of the account, where words end and the signs begin. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: From the word for a tether that keeps a camel from wandering. Reason in Arabic is a restraint on the self, so the challenge is about self-control as much as about intelligence.
A definite plural, so the threat is to place Moses inside an existing category of people already shut away. The word occurs nowhere else in the Quran in this form.

Pharaoh's condition for looking at the sign is that Moses belong to the truthful, which quietly makes the demonstration a test of character rather than of evidence. The word runs through the surah's other episodes too.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Threatening a troublesome speaker with confinement was familiar to the Meccans in a local form. A man who broke with his clan lost the protection that kept him alive, and the community had already tried a boycott, cutting a whole group off from trade and marriage for a period of years. Nobody in that audience needed the mechanics of the threat explained. They had watched a version of it work.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the imprisoned that Pharaoh threatens Moses with occurs in this form nowhere else in the Quran. Moses' two answers in this exchange each end on a condition about the listener rather than about God: if you were certain, and if you would use your minds. The description is given, and the capacity to receive it is placed on the other side.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Force enters the exchange the moment argument runs out, and the sequence is worth noticing: three answers, no reply to any of them, then a cell. The passage treats that as the natural progression rather than as a scandal. What follows is stranger. Moses does not withdraw and does not escalate; he offers evidence to a man who has just announced he will not be persuaded. The offer is made anyway, which is what being sent means here.

crossReferences.why: Shows the same court, with a threat to kill Moses and one man arguing against it.
Reports Pharaoh being shown nine clear signs and answering with the same accusation.
Uses the same imagery of prison, chosen there by a prophet over what he was being pressed to do.

studies.applyIt: Watch for the moment a disagreement stops being about the question. Someone raises their voice, or brings up your job, or says this is not up for discussion. That is the point where the argument ended. Notice it when it happens, without announcing it, and decide deliberately what to do next rather than escalating along with it.

studies.title: Named Magic On Sight
studies.meaning: Two signs, described in six words each. A staff becomes a serpent, plainly; a hand comes out white to whoever is looking. Neither is explained. Pharaoh's response is instant and it is not disbelief: he classifies. This is a skilled magician. Having named the category he moves to consequences, and the consequence he chooses is political. The man wants to drive you out of your land. Then he asks the court what to do, which turns a question about truth into a question about tactics.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Egypt was known throughout the region for its priestly craft, so magician was the available professional category for what Moses had just done, not an insult invented on the spot. The commentators note that Pharaoh's charge about the land is addressed to his nobles rather than to Moses, since a threat to property and position moves a court faster than a claim about God. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: A word for a full-sized snake rather than the small one another surah uses for the same event. The commentators reconcile them by size at different moments; the word occurs twice in the Quran.
The body of leading men around a ruler, the same word used for the notables of Mecca. It names those whose agreement a decision needs, which is why Pharaoh turns to them before acting.
The second word means learned, so the charge concedes expertise while denying the source. It is the most efficient form of dismissal available: not a fraud, a professional, and therefore explained.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The Quraysh made exactly this move about the Quran. It was called poetry, then soothsaying, then magic, and each label came with a known kind of person attached and a known way of discounting him. The classical sources report the Meccan leaders conferring before a pilgrimage season on which term to settle on, because the labels contradicted each other. Naming a thing was how an unfamiliar claim was kept from having to be answered.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for the serpent appears twice in the Quran and both times of this event, while two other surahs describe the same staff with a word for a small darting snake. The classical commentators treat the difference as stages of one transformation rather than as a discrepancy, and they say so openly rather than harmonising it away.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A sign is shown to be insufficient by itself. Two of them are given, both public and both immediate, and they change nothing, because a category was available that could absorb them. That is the passage's claim about evidence: what a person sees is filtered through what they already have a name for, and a name can be found for almost anything. The refusal then dresses itself as concern for the community's safety.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same two signs and the same charge, with the court repeating the fear about land.
Records Pharaoh calling the signs magic and proposing a contest at a fixed place.
Says they rejected the signs while inwardly certain of them, out of arrogance.

studies.applyIt: Catch yourself putting someone in a box today. He is just being defensive, she is only saying that because of her background, they are all the same. The box may even be accurate. Notice that the moment you close it, you stop having to consider what was actually said. Reopen one box before the day ends.

studies.title: Whoever Turns Out To Win
studies.meaning: The court's advice is procedural. Hold him off, send gatherers through the cities, bring back every expert. What follows is a state doing what states do: an appointment fixed for a known day, an announcement, a crowd assembled. Then the crowd's own sentence, which is the sharpest thing in the passage. We may follow the magicians, if they turn out to be the winners. Nobody has asked which side is right. The question is which side will hold the field.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The day named is identified in another surah as a festival, so the contest was staged when the population was already assembled and watching. The commentators note the political calculation: a public defeat of Moses in front of the whole city would settle the matter more thoroughly than a quiet arrest. No occasion is reported for these ayat, which move the account from a court exchange to a national event.

keyTerms.note: An imperative meaning to defer or keep waiting. The advice is not to answer Moses but to delay him, which buys the time the rest of the plan needs and concedes that no answer is ready.
An intensive form of the ordinary word, so not a magician but a great one. It occurs once in the Quran, and the escalation is in the grammar: Pharaoh's men want the best available, not merely more.
The word for winning a contest, not for being right. The crowd uses it, and then the magicians use it twice, and no word for truth appears anywhere in the arrangements being made.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca ran on public contests. Poets competed at the seasonal fair at Ukaz, crowds gathered, judgements were given, and a tribe's standing rose or fell with its champion. Everyone in that audience had watched a verdict follow a performance rather than an argument. The scene being described, a proclaimed day, a summoned crowd and a contest whose outcome would decide what people believed, was a familiar civic event.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the magicians Pharaoh's men want is an intensive form that occurs once in the Quran; everywhere else the ordinary word is used. The crowd's stated reason for coming is preserved without comment: they may follow the magicians if the magicians win. The Quran records the sentence and passes on, and the same crowd is not mentioned again.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Allegiance is shown attaching itself to outcome rather than to content, and the passage does not moralise about it. The crowd is not condemned; it is simply quoted, and the quotation does the work. What follows in the account undoes the calculation, since the side that wins is the side the crowd was not organised to support. But the disposition described here survives every result. People who follow winners will follow the next one too.

crossReferences.why: Sets the same appointment, naming the day as a festival and an open place.
Gives the same advice about summoning magicians and the same bargaining over reward.
Names the same logic in another form, following what the fathers did rather than what is shown.

studies.applyIt: Pick one opinion you hold and ask honestly when you started holding it. If the answer is around the time the people you respect started holding it, that is worth knowing. You do not have to change it. Just separate the two questions for a minute: is this true, and is this what my side says. They are not the same question.

studies.title: Is There A Reward For Us
studies.meaning: The magicians arrive and negotiate before they perform. Their first sentence is about the fee. Pharaoh raises the offer without being pressed, adding nearness to the throne to the money, which is the more valuable half. Then Moses gives them the floor with a courtesy that costs him nothing and concedes nothing: throw what you are going to throw. They do, and swear by Pharaoh's might as they do it, which names exactly what they are actually working for.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Court magicians in Egypt were professionals with a livelihood at stake, and the commentators read the opening question as ordinary contract negotiation rather than greed. The oath by Pharaoh's might is the only oath of its kind in the Quran, and the audience in Mecca swore by their own gods and their own chiefs in the same way. No occasion is reported for the exchange.

keyTerms.note: The commercial word for payment for work. It is the same word other prophets use when they refuse any, five times over in this surah, which sets the magicians' opening question against the surah's own refrain.
A court term for the inner circle admitted to the ruler's presence. The Quran uses the same word elsewhere for nearness to God, so the offer here is a smaller version of the thing it competes with.
An oath sworn by the power of a man. The phrase occurs once in the Quran, and the same word for might stands as one of God's names in the refrain that closes each episode of this surah.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Nearness to a chief was the real currency in Mecca too. A man's access to the men who decided things determined what he could charge, whom he could marry his daughters to and whether a grievance of his was heard. Money could be earned by anyone with a caravan share. Proximity could not, and it was understood to be the thing worth more, which is why Pharaoh offers it second.
studies.didYouKnow: The oath sworn here by a man's might occurs once in the Quran. The word for the nearness Pharaoh offers appears elsewhere for those brought near to God, including in the announcement made to Mary about her son. And the word for the fee the magicians ask about is the same one five prophets in this surah use to say they want none.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Everyone in the scene is working for something and the passage names each price without editorialising. The magicians want a fee and a place at court; Pharaoh wants a result and pays for it; the crowd wants to be on the winning side. Only Moses is described doing something with no stated return, and his single line does not argue, threaten or pray. He hands the floor to his opponents, which is what confidence in a case looks like.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same negotiation over payment and the same invitation to throw first.
Puts the refusal of any fee in Noah's mouth, the first of five identical statements here.
Records the same offer to throw first, with Moses answering that they may go ahead.

studies.applyIt: Write down what you are actually being paid for in the thing you spend most of your week on. Not the job title, the exchange: this much money, this much standing, this much of your attention. It is not a moral exercise and there is no correct answer. Most people have never put the terms of their own arrangement into a sentence.

studies.title: Thrown Down In Prostration
studies.meaning: Moses throws, and the staff begins swallowing what they had fabricated. Then the sentence that carries the whole scene: the magicians were thrown down prostrating. The verb is passive. They do not fall; they are put down, by the same word used four times in the preceding lines for casting a staff or a rope. And their first words name the Lord of the worlds, then correct themselves to make sure nobody thinks they mean Pharaoh: the Lord of Moses and Aaron.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. These were the professionals summoned from every city, the men best placed to know what a trick looks like, and the commentators make that the point of the story: the verdict comes from expert witnesses. The addition naming Moses and Aaron is explained as forestalling the obvious misreading, since Pharaoh claimed lordship himself and had done so in this surah. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: A verb for seizing something quickly with the mouth. It is used of this staff in three surahs and nowhere else, and it describes a taking in rather than a destroying.
A passive from the same verb used for throwing the staffs and ropes. The magicians are described as having been cast down rather than as having knelt, which puts the movement outside their decision.
From a root for turning a thing away from its proper direction, used of lies and of overturned towns. It names their work as inversion rather than as invention, and it occurs twice in the Quran.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An expert's public reversal was rare and expensive. A poet who conceded another's superiority at the fair lost commissions; a guide who admitted he had misread the stars did not lead again. The men in this scene had been brought in from every city, paid, and promised a place at court, and they gave all of it up in the length of one sentence, in front of the person who had hired them.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for throwing runs through five consecutive scenes of this account: Moses casts his staff, the magicians are told to cast, they cast, Moses casts again, and then they themselves are cast down. The last use is passive, and it is the only one where the thing thrown is a person.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Recognition is described as something that happens to a person rather than something they perform. The grammar does the theology: they are thrown down, and belief follows the body rather than preceding it. It also matters who these witnesses are. Nobody was better placed to explain the event away, and the ones who could not explain it were the ones who knew the craft. Expertise, here, is what makes the recognition credible.

crossReferences.why: Tells the same reversal, with the magicians naming the Lord of Moses and Aaron.
Uses the same verb for the staff swallowing, and reports the same prostration.
Gives Pharaoh's response and the magicians' answer, which is the rest of this scene.

studies.applyIt: Think of one thing you have been arguing for that you have quietly stopped believing. Say it to one person this week, plainly, without a long preamble about how you got there. The magicians change position in a single sentence and lose everything they were promised. Most of the cost people fear in changing their mind is the explaining.

studies.title: Before I Gave You Permission
studies.meaning: Pharaoh's first objection is not that they are wrong. It is that they did not ask. Belief is treated as an act requiring authorisation, which tells you what he thought he governed. Then the explanation: their teacher put them up to it, so the reversal becomes a plot rather than a verdict. Then the sentence, stated in exact detail: hands and feet cut on opposite sides, and crucifixion for all of them. Nothing in it addresses what the audience just watched.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The threat is reported in three surahs in almost identical words, which suggests it was a fixed part of the account. Cutting a hand and the opposite foot and then displaying the body was a recognised punishment for rebellion in the ancient Near East, aimed at the watching population rather than at the condemned. The Meccan audience was hearing this while some of its own were being tortured for the same reversal. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: From the root for hearing and for granting leave. Pharaoh's complaint is that a permission he issues was bypassed, which places the inner act of belief inside his jurisdiction.
The word for the eldest or the head of a group. Naming Moses their master turns a public defeat into an inside job, which is the cheapest available explanation and the one that saves most face.
A phrase specifying the right hand with the left foot. It occurs four times in the Quran, and three of those are this same threat by Pharaoh, told in three different surahs.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Punishment in that world was public by design. A body left where people passed was the announcement, and the point was not the offender but the crowd walking by. Mecca had its own version: the men and women who converted while owned were beaten in the open, on the hot ground outside the city, where everyone could see the price. The threat in this ayah was not exotic to the first listeners.
studies.didYouKnow: Pharaoh's threat appears in three surahs in nearly the same wording, and the phrase specifying opposite limbs occurs four times in the Quran, three of them attached to this same scene in three surahs. What varies between the tellings is what the magicians say back. The threat is fixed; the answer is given differently each time, and in this surah it is the briefest.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two mechanisms are on display and both are ordinary. Power that cannot answer a claim reclassifies it as conspiracy, which requires no evidence and explains everything. And it asserts authority over the interior, demanding permission for belief itself, which is the one place authority cannot reach. The threat that follows is an admission: the man who has to reach for the body has already lost the argument about the mind.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same accusation and threat, with a longer answer from the magicians.
Repeats the threat and adds the magicians' comparison between Pharaoh's power and God's.
States that there is no compulsion in religion, which is the principle this scene violates.

studies.applyIt: Notice who in your life needs to approve of a change before you are allowed to make it. Not who would be affected by it, who would have to sign it off in your head. Name the person. You may decide the approval is worth having. But the two questions are different, and most people never separate them.

studies.title: No Harm In That
studies.meaning: The answer to mutilation and death is two words: no harm. Then a reason that reframes the whole threat, that they are returning to their Lord in any case, and a hope that their wrongs will be forgiven because they were the first to believe. Minutes earlier they had been bargaining for a fee. The scene then cuts without transition to the departure at night and to Pharaoh's heralds going out again, this time to raise an army against a group he calls a small band.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The magicians' claim to be the first believers is understood by the commentators as first among Pharaoh's people, not first in the world. The night departure and the pursuit belong to the exodus, told at greater length elsewhere. The same word for heralds is used twice in this surah, once to summon magicians and once to summon soldiers, which puts the two mobilisations in the same words. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: A flat denial of injury, using a word that occurs once in the Quran. Two syllables answer a sentence of mutilation, and the brevity is the argument: the threatened loss is being priced at nothing.
From a verb for turning something over, so the return is a reversal rather than a journey. It is the ordinary word for going home, which makes death sound like the end of an errand.

A contemptuous word for a scrap of a group, occurring once in the Quran. Pharaoh uses it while raising an army against them, so the insult and the mobilisation contradict each other in the same speech.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Slaves and the poor made up much of the early Muslim community in Mecca, and several of them were held down in the sun and beaten to make them recant. The reports about that period are specific about who endured and who did not, and about the fact that some were bought out of it. An audience containing those people heard a story in which professionals lose everything in an afternoon and call it no harm.
studies.didYouKnow: Two words in this passage occur nowhere else in the Quran: the magicians' denial that any harm is being done to them, and Pharaoh's contemptuous term for the group he is chasing. And the phrase they use for themselves, the first of the believers, appears in only one other place, where Moses says it of himself after asking to see God.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Threats work by controlling what a person values, and the answer here removes the lever rather than resisting the pressure. Nothing is denied about the punishment; what is denied is that it constitutes harm, on the ground that the destination was always the same. The hope expressed alongside it is not for rescue but for forgiveness, which is a different request entirely. Courage in this passage is a matter of accounting rather than of nerve.

crossReferences.why: Gives their reply at greater length, ending with a prayer for patience poured over them.
Records the same refusal, with the magicians telling Pharaoh to decree what he will.
Repeats the instruction to travel by night with the servants, in almost identical words.

studies.applyIt: Name the thing you are most afraid of losing, and then write down what would actually still be true the day after you lost it. Not a consolation, a list. Your name, the people who would still be there, the morning after. The magicians do that arithmetic in one sentence, and it is the arithmetic, not the bravery, that lets them answer.

studies.title: Gardens, Springs And Treasures
studies.meaning: Pharaoh's speech ends on two claims about feeling: they enrage us, and we are a vigilant multitude. Then the narration takes the sentence over. So We brought them out of gardens and springs, treasures and a noble station. The subject of the verb has changed without warning; the man who mobilised an army is now the one being removed. And the last line hands the same things to the people he had enslaved, in four words.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Egypt's wealth was proverbial in Arabia: the Nile's irrigated land, the granaries that fed the region, the treasure of a state older than memory. What the passage lists is not luxury but the basis of the country's power. The commentators discuss whether the inheritance was of Egypt itself or of a comparable land, and record both readings without settling on one. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: From a word for rage that fills the chest. It occurs once in the Quran, and it is Pharaoh's stated reason for pursuit: not danger, not policy, but the feeling their leaving produced.
A participle for a body kept ready against a threat. It occurs once in the Quran, and it sits oddly beside the description of the departing group as a scrap of a band.
A place of standing, and by extension a position of honour. Listed after gardens, springs and treasures, it names the one item on the list that cannot be inherited by simply occupying it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccans knew Egyptian abundance at second hand and constantly. Grain reached the Hijaz from the Nile, and the northern caravan brought back what a valley of stone could not produce. A merchant who had seen the irrigated fields once described them for the rest of his life. Setting gardens, springs and treasures side by side was, to that audience, a list of everything their own city lacked.
studies.didYouKnow: Both words Pharaoh uses about his own state in this passage occur once each in the Quran: the rage he says the departure has caused, and the wariness he claims for his forces. He describes his feelings twice in two lines while calling the other side a scrap of a band, and the Quran lets the two statements stand next to each other.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Possession is described as tenancy. Everything listed was real and was held, and none of it was owned in any sense that survived a change of occupant; the same gardens and springs pass to the people who had worked them in chains. The passage makes no claim that wealth is bad. It makes a claim about duration, and about who does the transferring, which is stated as an act of God rather than as a turn of events.

crossReferences.why: Lists the same gardens, springs and noble station left behind, and says another people inherited them.
Says the oppressed inherited the east and west of the land that had been blessed.
Promises in advance that the weakened would be made leaders and inheritors.

studies.applyIt: Look around the room you are in and pick the thing you would least like to lose. Now ask who had it before you, or who made it, and who will have it after. Not to feel bad about owning it. Just to place it accurately in time. This passage lists real wealth and then changes whose name is on it in one line.

studies.title: My Lord Is With Me
studies.meaning: The two forces come into sight of each other and the people with Moses do the arithmetic out loud: we are caught. It is not panic; it is an accurate reading of the position, water ahead and an army behind. Moses answers with the same flat particle God had used to his own fear at the start, and then with a claim rather than a plan. My Lord is with me; He will guide me. The instruction to strike arrives only after that.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, at the point in the surah where the longest account reaches its crisis. The commentators emphasise the sequence: the assurance is spoken before any way out exists, and the command to strike comes afterwards. That order matters for an audience in Mecca with no visible exit of its own. The parting is described in one image, each part standing like a great mountain. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: A passive participle for being reached by a pursuer. It occurs once in the Quran, and it states a fact rather than a fear: at that distance they were within reach.
A future verb with no object supplied. Moses does not say to what, which leaves the assurance as a direction rather than a destination, and the sea is not mentioned until the next line.
A word for a high, immovable mass of rock. It occurs once in the Quran, and it is applied to water, which makes the sea take on the property most opposite to it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Being caught in open country was the specific fear of every caravan. Raiders picked their moment where there was no cover and no way round, and a merchant train that saw dust behind it on a plain had already lost. Everyone in the audience had either travelled under that threat or paid someone to guard against it. Water ahead and riders behind was a picture they could complete themselves.
studies.didYouKnow: Two words in this short passage occur once each in the Quran: the being overtaken, and the mountain the parted water is compared to. A third, the pursuit at sunrise, appears in only one other place, where it names the hour a town was destroyed. The same word carries a rescue here and an ending there.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The assurance is given before the solution exists, and the order is the teaching. Moses is not shown a way out and then reporting confidence; he states that God is with him while facing water, and the parting follows. That makes trust a position taken in the absence of evidence rather than a conclusion drawn from it. And the verb he uses is about being guided, not about being rescued, which leaves the form of the help open.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same crossing, with a dry path struck through the sea and the pursuit behind.
Uses almost the same words of assurance, spoken to a frightened companion in hiding.
Recalls the parting and the drowning in a single sentence addressed to a later generation.

studies.applyIt: Say the difficult thing out loud before you know how it ends. Not a prediction that it will work out, and not a plan. Just the sentence that God is with you in this, spoken while the problem is still exactly as large as it was. Then go back to the practical steps. Moses says it before the sea moves, not after.

studies.title: Ending On The Merciful
studies.meaning: Four short lines finish the longest account in the surah. The pursuers are brought near, which reads at first as an advantage and turns out to be the trap; those with Moses are saved, all of them; then the others are drowned. No detail is given, no scene of the water closing. And the last two lines are the refrain, which arrives here for the second time and ends, as it always does, on mercy after a drowning.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The refrain that closes this passage will close each of the six accounts that follow, always in the same two sentences. The commentators note the restraint of the narration here: other surahs describe Pharaoh's last words and the preservation of his body, and this one gives three verbs and stops. The account has been about speech throughout, and it ends by refusing to describe. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: A verb for bringing something close. This form occurs once in the Quran, and the same root returns later in this surah, where the garden is brought near to the God-conscious. Here the nearness given is to a drowning.
From a root for reaching high ground out of a flood or a danger. Deliverance in Arabic is spatial before it is spiritual: the saved are the ones who got clear.

Used twice in three lines for the pursuing army, and never named otherwise in this passage. Reducing Pharaoh and his forces to a pronoun withholds from them the attention the narrative gave them earlier.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabs on the coast knew drowning as the sea's ordinary business. Pearl divers and boat crews on the Red Sea lost men every season, and the word carried none of the distance it has for an inland reader. But the audience was also being told, by a surah that keeps closing on mercy, that the account of a destruction was not the last word being said. That combination was the unusual part.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for bringing the pursuers near occurs once in the Quran in this form, and the same root returns later in this surah for the garden being brought near to the God-conscious. One approach ends in water and the other in a garden, and the Arabic uses the same movement for both.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The refrain does the theological work. A story of drowning is closed with a sentence naming God as Mighty and as Merciful, and the second name is not softened or qualified by the first. That refuses the obvious division, where power handles the punishment and mercy handles the rescue. Both names are said over the whole event. What the surah asserts is that the two are not in tension, and it asserts it by repetition rather than by argument.

crossReferences.why: Gives Pharaoh's final words and the promise that his body would be preserved as a sign.
Uses the same root for bringing near, there of the garden approaching the God-conscious.
Names the deliverance of the Children of Israel from a humiliating punishment in two lines.

studies.applyIt: Read the last two lines of this passage twice today, once in the morning and once before you sleep. They are the same words each time and they close every story in this surah. Notice what changes between the two readings. It is a small experiment in what repetition does, and it is the method the surah itself is using on you.

studies.title: Do They Hear You Calling
studies.meaning: The second account opens with an instruction to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him): recite to them the news of Abraham. What follows is not a narrative but a cross-examination. Abraham asks what they worship, and their answer is oddly frank, that they worship idols and remain sitting beside them. Then two questions with no rhetoric in them. Do they hear you when you call? Can they help or harm? The questions are not about theology. They are about function.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Abraham was the ancestor the Quraysh claimed and the founder of the sanctuary they administered, which made an account of him refusing idols uncomfortable in a specific way. The commentators note that the surah gives no miracles in this episode, only conversation. The father is addressed alongside the people, and the Quran does not identify him further than that. No occasion is reported for the passage.

keyTerms.note: Not any information but news of consequence, the kind that changes what a listener does. The instruction is to recite it, so the story is presented as something delivered rather than told.
To remain in one place in attendance on something. The Quran uses it of devotion in a mosque as well as here, so the word describes the posture without judging the object.
Shaped figures rather than unworked stones. The indefinite plural appears twice in the Quran, and both times it is Abraham asking his people what exactly it is they are attending to.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The Kaaba in Mecca held images, and the families who tended them drew income and standing from the pilgrimage they attracted. Idols were not private objects; they were civic institutions with keepers, offerings and a calendar. Asking whether they could hear was therefore not an abstract question in that city. It was a question about an industry, put in front of the people who ran it.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the idols here appears in this indefinite form twice in the Quran, and both occurrences are Abraham putting the same question to his own people. The word for their sitting beside the images is used elsewhere in the Quran for people keeping to a mosque, so the Arabic gives the two practices the same verb and lets the difference lie in the object.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Abraham does not begin with a doctrine. He begins by asking what the thing does, which turns the question of worship into a question anybody can answer from experience. That approach assumes the listener is capable of the reasoning and has simply never been asked to do it. It also locates the error precisely: not in sincerity, since their devotion is real and constant, but in the object receiving it.

crossReferences.why: Records the same question to his father, followed by the reasoning through star, moon and sun.
Puts the same challenge about idols, ending with a claim about who made the heavens.
Gives the conversation with his father in gentler terms, asking why he serves what cannot hear.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you give steady time to and ask Abraham's question about it, plainly. What does it actually do for me. Not what it stands for, what it does. A subscription, a routine, a running argument, an account you check hourly. The point is not to stop. It is to have answered the question once, in your own words.

studies.title: They Are Enemies To Me
studies.meaning: Their defence is not an argument. We found our fathers doing it, which concedes everything Abraham asked and answers none of it. His reply does not attack the fathers. He widens the question instead, taking in everyone worshipped by them and by the generations before, and then says something startling: all of them are enemies to me. Not useless, not false. Enemies. And then the one exception, described by what He does rather than by a name.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Inherited practice was the strongest argument available in that society, since a man's religion arrived with his lineage and abandoning it meant declaring his ancestors wrong. The Quran records the same defence from the Quraysh in several places. The commentators note that Abraham's answer does not deny the ancestry; it denies that ancestry settles the question. No occasion is reported for these ayat.

keyTerms.note: A superlative for the most remote in time. It occurs once in the Quran, and it extends the argument past the fathers anyone could remember to the ones nobody could check.

Singular, though it refers to many, which Arabic allows when a class is meant. The word claims active hostility rather than mere emptiness, and the commentators read it as what the objects will prove to be on the day of reckoning.
A present tense, so the guiding is ongoing rather than finished. It opens a run of verbs that continues for several ayat, each naming something God does for Abraham in the present.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A Meccan's obligations were inherited whole: the clan he defended, the well he drew from, the images his family tended, the feuds he was born into. None of it was chosen and all of it was binding, and the man who stepped out lost the entire package at once. When Abraham's people say they found their fathers doing this, they are not being lazy. They are naming the only ground anyone in that world stood on.
studies.didYouKnow: The superlative Abraham uses for the earliest ancestors occurs once in the whole Quran. The line that follows it begins a sequence in which God is described only by verbs, one after another, with no adjectives and no names at all until the sequence ends. Each verb is in the present tense, so the description is of what is happening rather than of what was done once.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two moves are made and both are permanent. The first refuses inheritance as evidence: what your fathers did is a fact about them, not about the world, and the number of generations behind a practice adds nothing to its truth. The second replaces a noun with a series of verbs. God is not introduced by title but by what He is doing, which makes the relation continuous and leaves nothing to be looked at or handled.

crossReferences.why: Records the same appeal to what the fathers were found doing, and the answer given to it.
Continues Abraham's sequence of verbs, from feeding and healing to forgiveness.
Names Abraham as an example in exactly this separation from what his people served.

studies.applyIt: Find one practice in your life that you do because it was done at home. It might be good. It might be a way of arguing, a way of spending, a way of treating a certain kind of person. Ask, once, whether you would choose it now if it arrived without the family attached. Then decide, and let the decision be yours.

studies.title: When I Am Sick He Heals
studies.meaning: Abraham argues for one God from his own body rather than from the sky. He lists what is done for him in a rising order: food, water, healing, dying, being raised, and finally forgiveness, which he alone is uncertain of. One line breaks the pattern. Every other action is attributed to God, but the sickness is attributed to himself. The commentators read this as courtesy of speech rather than a claim about causes, since illness is no less under God's arrangement than recovery.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Surah 26 sets out a sequence of prophets who were rejected by their people, each account closing with the same refrain, and Abraham's comes after those of Moses. He is speaking to his father and his people about the images they served. The Meccan audience traced both their descent and their sanctuary to Abraham, so hearing him dismantle inherited worship placed them awkwardly inside a story they claimed as their own.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to bring something to its edge or brink, and so to recovery. Healing is pictured as arrival at a boundary, the point where an illness is crossed rather than merely eased.
The verb carries eager wanting and even greed. Used of forgiveness by a prophet, it keeps the outcome open, since one does not covet what one already holds.
From the root of ruling and of the bridle that steadies a horse. It names the capacity to decide rightly and to restrain, not information held.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In that country food and water were never assumed. A caravan measured its own life in waterskins, and a well fouled or a season without rain emptied a settlement. Medicine was thin: cauterising, cupping, honey, and waiting. A fever ran its course and the family watched. Naming feeding, watering and healing in one breath named the three things a person could least secure by their own effort.
studies.didYouKnow: Surah 26 is among the longest of the Meccan surahs, with 227 ayat, and its prophet narratives are separated by an identical two-line refrain praising God as the Mighty and the Merciful. The refrain returns eight times, so the surah is built as a series of panels, each closed by the same words before the next begins.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The case for one God is made here from breakfast and illness rather than from the order of the heavens, which puts the argument within reach of anyone. There is also a limit set at the end. Abraham, speaking as a prophet, describes forgiveness as something he hopes for and not something he counts on, so confidence in God's mercy is kept distinct from certainty about oneself.

crossReferences.why: Shows Abraham reasoning the other way, upward from the star, moon and sun to the One who made them.
Has Abraham ask to be shown how the dead are revived, the same item he lists here.
Records his parting words to his father, including the promise to ask forgiveness for him.

studies.applyIt: At your next meal, stop before the first mouthful and trace one item on the plate back three steps: who handled it, what field it grew in, what water fell there. Take about a minute. Abraham's argument begins exactly here, with the ordinary supply that arrives without your arranging it, and it is easier to follow after you have done the tracing once.

studies.title: Neither Wealth Nor Children
studies.meaning: Five requests follow one another, and their order carries the sense. Abraham asks first to be spoken of truly by people not yet born, then for the Garden, then for his father, then not to be shamed on the day of resurrection. The last line explains what will make shame possible: the two assets that ordinarily shield a person, wealth and sons, will not be in play. What he asks for at the start is therefore the only thing on the list that outlasts the day being described.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The passage continues Abraham's speech within Surah 26's sequence of rejected prophets. His plea for his father is treated elsewhere in the Quran as belonging to a period before it became clear that his father would not turn, and the text says he withdrew from it once that was settled. The surah addresses a Meccan audience for whom lineage and inherited standing were the strongest arguments available.

keyTerms.note: Literally a truthful tongue among later people. The request is not for fame but for accuracy: that what is eventually said of him should be true, whether or not it is flattering.

From inheritance law, where property passes to those who survive. Applying the word to the Garden treats it as something received rather than earned, arriving through a relationship instead of a purchase.
From a root meaning to be brought low in public view. What is feared is exposure before onlookers, not pain, which fits a society where standing was held in the eyes of others.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Without writing, a man survived only in speech. Genealogists held the lines of descent in memory and poets fixed reputations in verse that travelled with caravans. Wealth and sons were the two measures that made a man safe: sons to defend and to inherit, wealth to feed guests and pay compensation. The closing line names precisely the assets that made a person untouchable in that world.
studies.didYouKnow: This request is answered in the Quran itself. In Surah 19, at ayah fifty, God says that Abraham and his line were given a truthful tongue, lofty, using the same two-word phrase Abraham uses here in his prayer. The petition and the response are recorded in different surahs, with the wording preserved between them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The prayer treats the next life as continuous with this one, running from reputation through family to judgement without a break, and then removes two of the standing currencies at the final line. That the request for a father is included is significant in itself: concern for others is carried into a prayer about one's own standing, and the boundary between them is not drawn where a self-interested account would draw it.

crossReferences.why: Grants exactly what is asked here, a truthful tongue among later generations, in the same words.
Explains the plea for his father and records that Abraham withdrew from it once the matter was clear.
Repeats the closing point: on that day no father will pay anything on behalf of his child.

studies.applyIt: Think of one person who has died and is still spoken of well by people who knew them. Identify the single habit that earned that, not the achievement, and do that thing once today: a call made, a debt of attention paid, a name remembered. Abraham asks for accurate memory rather than admiration, and accurate memory is built out of repetitions.

studies.title: Brought Near And Displayed
studies.meaning: Abraham's prayer ends on an exception. Nothing will help on that day except a person who arrives with a sound heart, and the word for sound is the one used of a body without injury or disease. Then two images, built on the same grammar. The garden is brought near for the God-conscious; the blaze is made visible to those who went astray. Neither is entered yet. And the question put to them is not about belief but about their gods: where are they, and can they help?
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The passage closes Abraham's long address, which had moved from questioning his people to praying for himself and his father. The commentators discuss the sound heart at length and broadly agree it means a heart free of idolatry and of ill will, without narrowing it further. The two scenes that follow are given in matched passive verbs, which is how the surah presents the day throughout. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: The word for a body free of injury or disease, from the root behind peace and submission. Applied to a heart it names health rather than achievement: an organ working as it was made to.
A passive verb of approach. The garden moves toward the person rather than the person toward it, and the same root was used earlier in this surah for the pursuers being drawn toward the sea.
From a root for coming out into open ground. The blaze is not approached but uncovered, so the two scenes differ in grammar: one comes closer, the other simply stops being hidden.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A sound animal was worth several times a flawed one, and buyers in an Arabian market checked teeth, hooves and wind before agreeing a price. The vocabulary of soundness came from that inspection, not from philosophy. To an audience that had spent mornings running a hand down a camel's leg, a heart described as sound was a heart that would pass the same examination.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for a sound heart occurs twice in the Quran, and both times it belongs to Abraham: once here in his own words, and once where it is said of him directly. The verb for the blaze being uncovered occurs twice as well, here and in a short Meccan surah about the day itself.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The condition named is a state, not a record. What is asked for is a heart that is sound, which is a description of condition rather than a tally of deeds, and it sets the standard somewhere a person cannot simply accumulate their way to. The two scenes that follow are then both passive: nothing here is achieved by the one being judged. And the closing question is put to the objects of worship, which lets the answer be silence.

crossReferences.why: Says of Abraham that he came to his Lord with the same sound heart named here.
Uses the same verb for the garden brought near, and describes who it is brought near for.
Contains the only other use of the verb for the blaze being made plainly visible.

studies.applyIt: Check one thing about your heart the way you would check a machine, without deciding whether you are a good person. Is there someone you would be glad to see fail. That is a fault in the mechanism, not a verdict on you. Name it today and leave it named. A sound heart is described here as a condition, and conditions can be worked on.

studies.title: By God, We Were Astray
studies.meaning: The verb chosen for what happens to them is unusual and physical: they are tumbled in, head over heels, along with those who misled them and the whole army of Iblis. Then the scene becomes an argument. They are quarrelling inside it, and the words the Quran records are not a plea. They are an admission, sworn with an oath: by God, we were plainly astray, when we made you equal with the Lord of the worlds. The confession is addressed to the idols, not to God.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The passage belongs to the scene Abraham had described in his prayer, and the surah stays inside it for several ayat before returning to the refrain. The commentators note that the ones quarrelling include both the worshipped and the worshippers, and that the Quran gives the losing side's own account of what went wrong rather than pronouncing it. No occasion is reported for these lines.

keyTerms.note: A doubled form built for the sound of it, describing something rolled over and over as it falls. It occurs once in the Quran, and the repetition in the letters carries the repetition in the motion.

A reciprocal form, so the dispute runs both ways. What the passage reports of the fire is not screaming but argument, which keeps the scene in the register of a courtroom rather than a torture chamber.
From the verb for levelling two things to the same height. It occurs once in the Quran, and it names the error precisely: not denying God but placing something alongside Him on the same line.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Oaths were the strongest instrument in Arabian speech. A man swore by God to close an argument nobody could otherwise settle, and swearing falsely was a serious matter with consequences that followed a family. The Quran here puts that oath in the mouths of people who have already lost everything, swearing to a fact that no longer helps them. To the first audience, the strongest available form arriving too late was the point.
studies.didYouKnow: Two words in these five lines occur nowhere else in the Quran: the verb for being tumbled in head over heels, and the verb for having made something equal with God. The first is a doubled form whose sound imitates the falling it describes. The second states the error in a single word, and it is spoken by the people who committed it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The confession names the error as equating rather than as denying, which is a precise and uncomfortable distinction. Nobody in the scene is quoted saying there was no God. What is admitted is that something was placed beside Him, which is a much easier thing to do and a much harder thing to notice. And the admission arrives at the point where it changes nothing, which is what makes it a description of the error rather than a repentance from it.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same quarrel between the followed and the followers, each blaming the other.
Records a similar exchange, ending with a speech in which the tempter denies any power over them.
Names people who take rivals beside God and love them as God should be loved.

studies.applyIt: Ask what sits beside God in your week rather than what replaces Him. Nobody reading this has another god. But something gets the first hour, the best attention, the anxious thought at three in the morning. Name that one thing today, without resolving to fix it. The word this passage uses is levelling, and levelling happens quietly.

studies.title: No Intercessor, No Close Friend
studies.meaning: The complaint shifts from self-accusation to blame: nobody misled us except the criminals. Then two absences are named, and the second is the surprising one. There is no intercessor, which is expected, and there is no devoted friend, which is not. The word is the ordinary one for a friend, the person who would stand up for you without being asked. Its absence is listed as a loss on the same page as an advocate's. Then a wish for a second run, and the refrain.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Intercession was a live expectation in Arabia, where the images at the Kaaba were understood by many as go-betweens who would put a case forward. The Quran addresses that expectation repeatedly. The mention of a friend belongs to a different register, since a man's standing in that world depended on people willing to speak for him without payment. Both supports are removed in two short lines. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to make a thing even by pairing it, so an intercessor joins himself to your case. The plural occurs twice in the Quran, both times in a sentence saying there are none.
The first word is the ordinary one for a friend and occurs in this form once in the Quran. The second means warm, from heat, so the friendship named is close rather than merely cordial.
A word for wheeling round and coming back, used of cavalry turning for a second charge. The wish is not for forgiveness but for another attempt, which is a request for time rather than mercy.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A man in Mecca survived on people who would speak for him. If he was accused, killed or ruined, what happened next depended on whether anyone stood up: a clan chief, a protector, a friend with standing.
