There were no courts and no police, only the willingness of others to intervene. Losing every person who would speak for you was not an abstraction in that city. It was the definition of being finished.
studies.didYouKnow: The plural for intercessors occurs twice in the Quran and both times inside a sentence denying there are any. The ordinary word for a friend appears in this exact form once. And the word for the second chance being wished for is the one used of horsemen wheeling round to charge again, so the request is phrased as a return to the field.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Naming a friend alongside an advocate says something about what people are actually for. An intercessor is a mechanism; a friend is a relation, and the passage counts the loss of both. That treats human closeness as a real good rather than a distraction from God, which is why its absence can be named as part of the loss. The wish that follows asks for repetition, and the surah answers by moving to the next story.

crossReferences.why: Says close friends will be enemies to one another on that day, except the God-conscious.
Contains the only other use of the plural for intercessors, in a similar admission.
Records the same wish to be sent back, and says they would return to what they left.

studies.applyIt: Think of one person who would speak for you if you were not in the room, and do something small for them this week. A message, a favour, an hour. This passage counts a friend as a thing that can be lost, in the same breath as an advocate. Friendships are maintained or they are not, and nobody notices the maintenance until it stops.

studies.title: Their Brother Noah
studies.meaning: The refrain closes Abraham's account and the next one begins in the same breath. The people of Noah denied the messengers, in the plural, though only one came to them. Then a formula that will be repeated three more times in this surah with different names inserted: their brother said to them, will you not be wary? Noah's three sentences contain no theology. He states his relation to them, claims to be trustworthy, and asks for two things: wariness of God, and their attention.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Noah's account is the first of five that follow the same template: the people denied, a man of their own spoke, he claimed to be trustworthy, he asked for no payment, they refused, and the refrain closed the section. The commentators note that the word brother here means one of them by descent, not by faith, which is what makes the refusals a matter of a community rejecting its own. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: Kinship by descent, not by belief. The phrase occurs four times in the Quran and all four are in this surah, introducing four of the prophets; the fifth is introduced without it.
From the root behind safety and faith, so the word means someone with whom a thing is safe. The phrase claiming it occurs five times in this surah, once in each account.
A verb for compliance with a person. It is paired every time with wariness of God, so obedience to the messenger is never asked for on its own account in these passages.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) had been known in Mecca as the trustworthy one before he said anything about revelation, and the Quraysh had used him to arbitrate. That reputation was a fact about him that his opponents could not withdraw. Hearing five earlier prophets each open by claiming exactly that word, an audience in Mecca was being told that the sequence had a place already prepared for the man in front of them.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase naming a prophet as the people's own brother occurs four times in the Quran and every one is in this surah. The claim to be a trustworthy messenger occurs five times here and once elsewhere. Four of the five accounts open with a man of the people's own blood; the fifth prophet is introduced by name alone, without the word for brother.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The template itself is the argument. By running five prophets through the same six sentences, the surah makes the pattern visible in a way a single story could not: the message is constant, the resistance is constant, and the differences between the peoples turn out not to matter. It also grounds prophecy in kinship. The one sent is a brother, from inside the community, which removes any excuse that he could not understand them.

crossReferences.why: Opens the next account with the same words, replacing the name with that of another prophet.
Gives Noah's message in his own surah, with the same three requests in the same order.
Tells the same account at greater length, including the reply of Noah's people.

studies.applyIt: Notice how often you refuse advice because of who is giving it. A sibling, a colleague you have known too long, someone whose own life is untidy. Take one piece of advice you dismissed for that reason and consider it again on its own, for two minutes. These accounts turn on people refusing a brother, and the brother part is why.

studies.title: What Do I Know Of Them
studies.meaning: Noah repeats the disclaimer that will be repeated four more times in this surah, once by each of the prophets who follow: I ask you no payment. Then the objection, and it is about class. Shall we believe you when the lowest sort follow you? Noah's answer refuses the question twice over. He does not defend his followers, and he does not accept that their standing is his business. Their account is with my Lord, not with me.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The same objection was being made in Mecca, where the early community included slaves, freedmen and men without clan backing, and the leadership is reported to have asked that these be sent away before any conversation could happen. The commentators connect the two directly. Noah's reply, which declines to assess anybody's worth, is preserved in almost the same words in another surah. No occasion is reported for this passage.

keyTerms.note: A superlative for the most contemptible, applied to people by rank rather than by conduct. It occurs once in the Quran, and it is a word about who someone's parents were.
A word from arithmetic, the same one used for settling a debt. Placing the followers' accounts with God removes them from the prophet's ledger as well as from the objectors'.
A verb for noticing something by feel rather than by reasoning it out. Noah ends on the softer word, so the rebuke is that they have not registered the point rather than that they cannot follow it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Rank in Mecca was visible in everything: where a man sat, whom he could marry, whether his testimony carried. Early converts included people at the bottom of that order, and the reports describe the leading men objecting to sitting alongside them. A message that arrived without asking about lineage was, for the people it reached first, the first thing in their lives that had not.
studies.didYouKnow: The word the objectors use for Noah's followers occurs once in the whole Quran. It is a superlative about social rank, not about behaviour, and Noah does not dispute it; he says he has no knowledge of what they do. The same disclaimer about payment that opens this passage appears five times in this surah, always in identical words.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Noah is offered an easy defence and declines it. He could have argued that his followers are better than they look, which would have accepted the premise that their worth was on trial. Instead he says he does not know what they do and that their reckoning is not his. That places the assessment of persons outside human competence altogether, including the prophet's. It also removes the only condition on which the objectors were willing to listen.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same objection about the lowly followers and Noah's refusal to drive them away.
Instructs that those who call on their Lord morning and evening are not to be dismissed.
Tells the listener to keep his eyes on such people rather than on those with wealth.

studies.applyIt: Notice whose opinion you weigh by their position rather than their point. The junior person in the meeting, the relative without a degree, the neighbour whose house is a mess. Take one thing said by someone in that category this week and consider it as if a person you respect had said it. Nothing more. Just run the sentence through the other filter.

studies.title: Judge Between Me And Them
studies.meaning: Noah answers the demand to send his followers away with a refusal and a job description. I am not one to drive believers off; I am only a plain warner. The threat that comes back is physical: stop, or you will be among the stoned. Then he turns away from them entirely and speaks to God, and the prayer has two halves. Decide between me and them, decisively. And deliver me, and whoever is with me of the believers.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Stoning was the ordinary way a community expelled or killed someone it had cast out, carried out collectively so that no one hand was responsible. The Quran reports the same threat being made to other prophets. The commentators note that Noah prays only after every argument has been made and refused, and that the prayer asks for a decision rather than for a punishment. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: A participle for chasing something off, used of shooing an animal. Noah denies being that kind of person rather than denying the request, so the refusal is put as a fact about his character.
A definite plural, so the threat is to add him to a group that already exists. The word occurs once in the Quran, and stoning was a collective act with no single author.
From the verb for opening. Judging in Arabic is opening a thing that was closed, and the noun repeats the verb here to make the decision final rather than provisional.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Expulsion was the real weapon in Arabia, and stoning was its final form. A man without a clan behind him could be killed by anyone with no consequence, so the threat of being driven out was a death sentence with a delay. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was stoned at Taif when he took the message outside Mecca, and the reports about that day were part of what the first audience brought to this passage.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for those who are stoned occurs once in the Quran, in this threat. Noah's prayer uses a verb from the root for opening, which is also the root behind the surah that opens the Book and behind the word for a decisive victory. Judging, opening and winning are the same three letters in Arabic.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Noah is asked to buy an audience by discarding the people who already believed, and the price is refused without negotiation. That establishes something about how a community is formed: it cannot be traded up. When the prayer finally comes, it asks for a decision and for deliverance, in that order, and it does not ask for anyone's destruction. What is wanted is an end to the deadlock rather than a verdict against them.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same prayer in four words, that he is overcome, so help him.
Records the same refusal to drive away the believers, with Noah's reasons stated at length.
Gives a later and harder prayer from Noah, after the same long refusal.

studies.applyIt: Think of a room you would get into if you left one person out of the story. A friend who embarrasses you, a relative, a part of your own history. Then do not leave them out, once, this week. Noah is offered access on exactly that condition and declines it in half a sentence.

studies.title: The Ark, Fully Laden
studies.meaning: The deliverance takes one line and the drowning takes four words. No storm is described, no waiting, no door closing. What the passage does give is an adjective: the ship was loaded, filled to capacity, which is the only detail supplied about the vessel the whole tradition builds on. Then the refrain, for the third time. And then, without a break, the next people are named and the same sentence starts again with a different nation in it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Other surahs give the flood at length, with the building of the ark, the mockery it drew and the son who would not board. This surah gives none of it, because the sequence is the point: seven accounts in the same shape, told fast enough that the shape becomes visible. The commentators note the compression as deliberate rather than as an abbreviation. No occasion is reported for these ayat.

keyTerms.note: A passive participle for a ship packed with cargo. It occurs three times in the Quran, twice of this ark and once of the vessel that carried Jonah, and it is the only description the ark is given here.

Those left over. The word occurs twice in the Quran, and in the other place it names Noah's descendants as the ones who continued, so the same word covers those who were left behind and those who remained.
An Arabian people placed by the commentators in the sand country of the south. They are named without introduction, on the assumption that the audience already knows who they were.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A loaded ship was a specific sight to Arabs on the Red Sea coast: hull low in the water, cargo lashed down, nothing more able to be put aboard. Traders knew exactly how much a vessel could take before it stopped being safe. Calling the ark loaded says it was carrying its limit, which is a different image from the enormous empty vessel later paintings supply.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the laden ship occurs three times in the Quran: twice of Noah's ark and once of the ship Jonah sailed on. The word for those left to drown here occurs twice, and its other use names Noah's own descendants as the ones who remained. The Arabic gives survival and abandonment the same participle.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Withholding the drama is itself a statement. A story told this fast cannot be enjoyed, and the surah keeps refusing to let the reader settle into any single account. What is left after the compression is the structure: a message, a refusal, an end, and a sentence about mercy. Placing the same refrain after each one asserts that the outcome is not a series of separate divine moods but one consistent way of dealing.

crossReferences.why: Gives the whole flood in detail, from the building of the ark to the landing.
Uses the same word for those who remained, applied there to Noah's descendants.
Names the same laden ship as a sign, and mentions what was made like it.

studies.applyIt: Try telling the story of a hard year of your life in four sentences, out loud, with no scenes in it. What happened, what you did, how it ended, what it means now. The compression will annoy you, and that is the exercise. This surah tells seven of the largest stories it has that way, and the shape is what it wants you to see.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: A Marker On Every Height
studies.meaning: The template runs again with a new name in it: their brother Hud, will you not be wary, I am a trustworthy messenger, fear God and obey me, I ask you no payment. Four sentences, identical to Noah's. Then the fifth line breaks the pattern, and it is a question about architecture. Do you build a landmark on every high place, for amusement? The charge is not idolatry. It is building for the sake of being seen.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Aad were an Arabian people whose ruins the Quran places in the sand country to the south, and the commentators describe them as builders and as physically imposing. What the passage objects to is specific: structures raised on high ground with no use, which the classical readings gloss as towers, pigeon houses or monuments. The word for the high place occurs once in the Quran, so the tradition works from context. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: Raised land, a ridge or a rise. It occurs once in the Quran, and the commentators offer several readings of what was built there, recording the range rather than settling it.
A verb for aimless activity with no purpose behind it. It occurs once in the Quran, and it is the charge: not that the buildings were wrong but that they were for nothing.
The same word the Quran uses for a verse and for a sign in nature. Here it means a structure meant to be noticed, so the object of the question is something built purely to signify.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Building on a ridge was visible from a day's ride away. In open country a structure on high ground announced who held the territory, and travellers navigated by them. Mecca itself had almost no monumental building; the Kaaba was modest and the houses were low. To an audience with nothing to point at, a people who put markers on every rise sounded less impressive than strange.
studies.didYouKnow: Two words in the last line of this passage occur once each in the whole Quran: the word for the high ground and the verb for doing something idly. The four lines before it are word for word the same as four lines spoken by Noah eighteen ayat earlier, with one name changed. The repetition is exact and the departure from it is immediate.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The objection is aimed at purpose rather than at the object. Building is not condemned; building for no reason is, and the word used means play. That makes the charge available to anyone, since most of what people accumulate is for being seen rather than for being used. It also arrives before any mention of idols in this account, which puts the misuse of effort ahead of the misdirection of worship.

crossReferences.why: Names Aad and the city of pillars, described as never having been built anywhere else.
Tells the same account, with Hud reminding them of their strength and their size.
Names the competition in accumulation that occupies people until the graves.

studies.applyIt: Look at one thing you own or maintain and ask whether anyone would notice if it were gone. Not whether it is expensive. Whether it does anything. A room you keep for guests who do not come, a subscription, a version of yourself online. Keep it if you want. But answer the question first, in words, today.

studies.title: He Supplied You, And You Know
studies.meaning: Two more charges and then a turn. You take strongholds as if you will live forever; when you seize, you seize like tyrants. Then Hud stops accusing and starts listing. Be wary of the One who supplied you with what you know, and the sentence repeats the verb rather than continuing it: He supplied you with livestock and children. The accusation and the inventory use the same grammar, and the inventory is longer.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The commentators describe Aad as a people of unusual strength who used it without restraint, and the passage names both the strength and its manner. The word for their fortifications occurs once in the Quran and the classical readings range over water-works, castles and workshops. What follows is a list of ordinary blessings put in the same sentence as the accusation, which the commentators read as the argument's actual weight. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: From the verb for making or manufacturing. It occurs once in the Quran, and the classical commentators read it variously as fortresses, cisterns or workshops, recording the alternatives without choosing.

A verb for taking hold violently and suddenly. Repeating it with the adverb makes the manner the charge: not that they struck, but how, and the word for tyrants describes the grip rather than the office.

keyTerms.gloss: He supplied you, extended to you
keyTerms.note: From the verb for stretching something out, so the supply is continuous rather than a single gift. The word occurs twice in the Quran, in consecutive ayat here, the second repeating the first and then naming what was given.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Livestock and sons were the two forms of wealth an Arabian actually counted. Camels were capital, transport and food at once, and a man with sons had labour, defence and a name that would continue. Nobody in that audience needed to be told these were valuable. Naming them as things that were supplied rather than earned was the part that landed, because both looked to their owners like the result of good management.
studies.didYouKnow: Two words in these lines occur once each in the Quran: the term for the works they built, and the verb for living forever that describes what they hoped from them. The verb for God supplying them occurs twice, and both occurrences are here, in consecutive lines, the second one repeating the first before it names anything.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument moves from what they did to what they were given, and that is the whole method. Nothing is said about their buildings being false or their strength imaginary. Both are conceded, and then attributed. The claim is not that they achieved nothing; it is that the raw material of every achievement arrived from somewhere. Gratitude, in this passage, is a matter of accurate attribution rather than of feeling.

crossReferences.why: Reports Aad asking who could be stronger than them, and names what actually was.
States that every blessing you have is from God, which is the move made here.
Gives the same mistake in a parable, a man whose garden convinced him it would never end.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you are proud of building and write the sentence before it. The teacher who let you in, the health you did not arrange, the family that fed you while you tried. Not to diminish the work. The work was yours. But this passage puts the achievement and the supply in the same sentence, and both halves are true.

studies.title: The Same Whether You Warn
studies.meaning: Hud finishes his list with gardens and springs and then names what he is afraid of on their behalf. The answer is the flattest refusal in the surah. It is all one to us whether you warn or do not; this is only what the ancients did; and we are not going to be punished. Three sentences, each removing a different thing: the speaker's effect, the message's novelty, and the outcome. Nothing is argued. Everything is dismissed.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The middle sentence is read two ways in the classical tradition, depending on how one word is voweled: either this is nothing but the habit of the ancients, or this is nothing but the ancients' invention. Both readings are preserved and both make the same move, which is to file the message under something already known. The Quraysh were making the same objection in Mecca. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.gloss: it is all one to us
keyTerms.note: A phrase of exact equivalence, from the verb for levelling. It says the warning has no weight in either direction, which is a stronger refusal than disagreement, because it declines to engage at all.
From a verb for counsel that moves the heart rather than instructing the mind. It occurs once in the Quran, and the objectors use it to reduce the whole message to a genre of speech.

The word can be voweled as custom or as fabrication, and both readings are preserved in the classical tradition. Either way it dates the message rather than answering it, which is the oldest form of dismissal.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Warning speech had a recognised place in Arabia. The soothsayer, the tribal orator and the wandering preacher all had their forms, and audiences knew how to sit through one politely and leave unchanged. Reducing a message to its genre was therefore easy and socially available: you did not have to argue with a warner, you only had to name him as one. The Quraysh used the same technique.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for those who admonish occurs once in the whole Quran, in this refusal. And the word for what they call the message has two accepted vowellings in the classical reading tradition, giving either the ancients' custom or the ancients' fabrication. The tradition preserves both without treating the difference as a problem to be resolved.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The refusal is complete because it is not an argument. Saying that it makes no difference whether you speak removes the possibility of being answered, and dating the message to the ancients removes the need to examine it. Then the third sentence states the conclusion as a fact about the future. What the passage records is not disbelief arrived at but disbelief already settled, and it is preserved in their own words rather than characterised.

crossReferences.why: States the same condition plainly, that warning them and not warning them are alike.
Records the Meccans dismissing the recitation as tales of the ancients.
Uses the same formula about warning making no difference to certain listeners.

studies.applyIt: Notice the sentence you use to close a subject you do not want opened. Everyone says that. I have heard it before. It is not that simple. They may all be true. But watch what they do, which is to end the conversation without answering it, and try going one sentence further the next time you reach for one.

studies.title: One Ending, One Beginning
studies.meaning: Aad's account closes in two words: they denied him, so We destroyed them. Then the refrain, twice as long as the ending it follows. Then the next people are named and their brother Salih says the same first sentence Noah and Hud said. The seam is visible here in a way it is nowhere else, because the destruction and the refrain and the new opening sit in three consecutive lines. The pattern is doing the arguing.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Thamud were the northern counterpart to Aad, an Arabian people whose rock-cut dwellings lay on the caravan route the Meccans travelled. The two are named together throughout the Quran. The commentators note that this surah gives Aad's destruction without describing it, where other surahs name a wind that blew for days, and read the omission as part of the sequence's pace. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: One verb for the whole outcome, with no instrument named. Other surahs give the wind and its duration; here the destruction is a single word placed immediately after the denial, with nothing between them.
A people of the northern Hijaz whose carved rock dwellings still stand. The Quran names them repeatedly, and always as a case the audience could go and look at.
The opening question of five accounts in this surah, unchanged each time. It asks about a disposition rather than a belief, and it is put before any doctrine is mentioned in any of them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A Meccan trader on the road north passed the Thamud site directly. Facades cut into cliff faces, doorways and chambers hollowed out of solid rock, and nobody living in them. The reports say travellers were told not to linger there. Two peoples, one to the south under sand and one to the north in stone, framed the trade routes on either side, and the Quran uses both as evidence the audience had already seen.
studies.didYouKnow: The destruction of a whole people is given here in two Arabic words, and the sentence about God that follows it is longer than the destruction itself. That proportion holds across the surah: each ending is brief and each refrain is fixed, so the space given to the outcome shrinks while the space given to the closing statement never changes.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing an ending and a beginning in adjacent lines makes a claim about history. Nothing is concluded by the destruction of Aad; the next sentence simply starts another people in the same position, which means the outcome was never the point of the telling. What repeats is the offer, and it is repeated to people who have every reason to know how it went last time. The refrain in between names mercy each time.

crossReferences.why: Names the wind that destroyed Aad and how long it blew, which this surah omits.
Tells the Thamud account at length, including the she-camel and the killing of it.
Places Aad and Thamud side by side and describes what each was warned about.

studies.applyIt: Read this passage aloud and stop at the line where one story ends and the next begins. It takes about ten seconds. Notice that nothing prepares you for the transition, and that the surah expects you to keep going. That expectation is the point, and it is the same expectation the passage has about people starting over after other people did not.

studies.title: Left Secure In What Is Here
studies.meaning: Salih finishes the shared opening and then asks a question nobody wants asked. Will you be left, in what is here, secure? The phrase is deliberately vague about what here means, and the three lines that follow fill it in: gardens, springs, cultivated fields, and date palms whose spathes are soft and heavy with fruit. Nothing in the list is criticised. The whole weight falls on one word, secure, and on the assumption that any of it stays.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Thamud's country in the northern Hijaz had water and cultivation, which is what made their settlements viable and their ruins striking. The commentators note that Salih's argument uses the prosperity itself rather than any wrongdoing: he asks whether the arrangement is permanent, not whether it is deserved. The word for the palm spathes occurs once in the Quran, which suggests a precise agricultural observation. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: From the root behind trust and faith, so security and belief share a word. The question is whether the safety they feel is a fact about the world or a feeling about it.
Used of a date palm's spathe when it is laden and yielding. It occurs once in the Quran, and it is the kind of detail a person notices only if they have handled the crop.

A demonstrative for the immediate surroundings, left undefined so it takes in whatever the listener happens to be counting. The list that follows supplies the content, but the word itself is deliberately open.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A date palm was a household's insurance. It fruited for decades, tolerated poor water, and its yield could be stored, traded and eaten through a bad year. A man counted his palms the way another might count savings. Naming the spathes as soft and heavy is a grower's detail, the moment before harvest when the crop is visibly there and not yet in hand, which is exactly when a person feels safest.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing the palm fruit here occurs once in the whole Quran. It is a technical term from date growing, and the Quran spends it on a single ayah in the middle of a warning. The list it belongs to, gardens and springs, is the same pair used of Hud's people a few ayat earlier, and earlier again of what Pharaoh's people lost.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The question is about duration, not about morality. Salih does not say the gardens were ill-gotten or that enjoyment is wrong; he asks whether being left in place is something anyone is owed. That relocates the argument from what people deserve to what people can count on, which is harder to dismiss because it does not accuse anybody. Security is treated as the real object of worship here, and it is named without being condemned.

crossReferences.why: Records the same argument in Mecca, that accepting the message would cost them their security.
Gives a town that was secure and content, and what happened to its provision.
Names security and food as the two things the Quraysh were given, and who gave them.

studies.applyIt: Write down the three things that make you feel your life is settled. A job, a lease, a person, a number in an account. Do not resolve to give any of them up. Just notice that you have never listed them before and that each one arrived from somewhere. Salih's question is only about how long, and it is worth sitting with for a minute.

studies.title: Do Not Obey The Wasteful
studies.meaning: Their skill is described before it is questioned. You carve houses out of the mountains with expertise, and the word used carries both craftsmanship and self-satisfaction at once. Then two instructions that sit oddly together. Obey me; and do not obey the command of those who go to excess, who spread ruin on the earth and do not set anything right. Salih is not asking for obedience in general. He is naming which instructions to refuse.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The rock-cut dwellings of Thamud in the northern Hijaz are still standing, carved into cliff faces along the route Meccan caravans took north, so the audience could picture the workmanship exactly. The commentators identify the extravagant ones Salih warns against as the leading men of the town, and another surah names nine men in the city who plotted. No occasion is reported for these ayat.

keyTerms.note: A participle read two ways by the commentators, as skilled and as exulting. Both are preserved, and the ambiguity is useful: the same word covers the craft and the pride in it. It occurs once in the Quran.
Not the greedy but those who exceed a limit, in spending or in anything else. The word appears seven times in the Quran, and it names a habit of overstepping rather than a particular sin.
An intensive passive form, so not merely enchanted but thoroughly worked upon. It occurs twice in the Quran and both are in this surah, said by two different peoples to two different prophets.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Carving a house out of living rock was not a shelter decision. It was a statement about permanence: a building that could not burn, could not be blown down and could not be dismantled by an enemy. Meccans built with mud brick and stone that a bad season could take. Passing a cliff face cut into rooms by people who were no longer there made a particular impression, and the Quran uses it repeatedly.
studies.didYouKnow: The word Salih's people throw back at him, calling him thoroughly bewitched, occurs twice in the Quran, and both occurrences are in this surah: here, and thirty-two ayat later when another people say the same thing to another prophet. The word for his skill in carving occurs once, and the commentators read it as both expertise and self-delight.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Obedience is treated as unavoidable and therefore as a choice of object. Salih does not tell them to stop following people; he tells them which people, and describes those people by what they produce rather than by what they believe. The test given is practical: do they set anything right, or do they only spread damage. That standard can be applied by anyone, without access to a person's intentions.

crossReferences.why: Names the nine men in the city who spread corruption and plotted against Salih.
Recalls the same carving of houses out of the mountains, alongside the plains they built on.
Describes people who claim to be putting things right while being the ones who spoil them.

studies.applyIt: Apply Salih's test to one voice you take seriously: a commentator, a manager, an account you read daily. Ask what that person has actually built or repaired, as opposed to what they have criticised. It is not a verdict on them. It is a way of deciding how much of your attention their instructions should get this month.

studies.title: A Turn At The Water
studies.meaning: The demand is for a sign and the objection behind it is that Salih is only a human being like them. What he produces is not a display. It is a she-camel and a timetable: she has a turn at the water, and you have a turn on a known day. The sign is an arrangement rather than an event, and it works only if it is kept. Then one prohibition, stated with a consequence and no further explanation.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Water rights were the hardest thing in Arabian life to settle, and a well or spring was often shared by rotation between families and their herds. The commentators describe the arrangement here in those terms: alternate days at the source, the camel taking one and the town the other. The Quran does not explain how the camel came, and the classical sources record differing accounts rather than one. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: A drinking turn, the recognised term for one party's allotted access to a shared source. It occurs four times in the Quran, and here it makes the sign a matter of scheduling rather than of spectacle.
The standing objection in this surah and elsewhere: a messenger who eats and needs water cannot be carrying anything more than a person carries. The Quran answers it by not disputing the description.

keyTerms.gloss: do not touch her with harm
keyTerms.note: The phrasing names harm by contact rather than a specific act. It is broad enough to cover driving her off, injuring her or killing her, and it leaves the whole question of restraint on one animal.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wells were the flashpoint of the desert. Rotation agreements between tribes were negotiated, remembered by name, and broken at the cost of blood, and a man who watered out of turn could start a feud that outlasted him. A camel needing its own share was not a small imposition; a full-grown animal drinks a great deal at once. The sign given here asked a whole town for restraint every second day.
studies.didYouKnow: The sign Salih is asked for turns out to be a rota. The word used for the drinking turn is the ordinary legal term Arabs used for shared access to a well, and it occurs four times in the Quran. Nothing about the camel's appearance is described anywhere in the Book; what is described is the schedule and the instruction attached to it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A sign is given in the form of a daily inconvenience. It cannot be watched and then forgotten, because keeping it requires a decision every second morning for as long as the animal lives. That makes it a test of a community rather than a demonstration to individuals, and it puts the burden on the many rather than on the one asked to believe. The eventual failure is therefore collective, and so is the warning attached.

crossReferences.why: Names the same camel as a test and states the division of the water between the two turns.
Calls the camel a sign and gives the same instruction about letting her graze freely.
Repeats the warning against touching her with harm, followed by the same consequence.

studies.applyIt: Find the standing arrangement in your household that only works if everyone keeps it: the bin, the shared drive, the parking space, whose turn it is. Keep your part of it exactly this week, including the day it is inconvenient. The sign in this passage was a rota, and the failure, when it came, was one act on one morning.

studies.title: Regret The Next Morning
studies.meaning: They hamstrung her, and the next word is that they became regretful. The order matters: the regret is real and it is immediate and it changes nothing, because the sentence after it is that the punishment took them. Regret is presented here as a feeling that arrived on time and did nothing, which is a harder thing to read than defiance would have been. Then the refrain, and then the next people are named.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The verb for what they did to the camel is a specific one, used of cutting the tendons of a standing animal so that it falls, and the Quran uses it of this event in three surahs. Other passages say one man carried out the act while the people were held responsible for it. The commentators note the plural here, and read it as consent rather than as many hands. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: A verb for severing the leg tendons so an animal collapses where it stands. It occurs three times in the Quran, always of this camel, and it names a killing that is slow and deliberate.
A participle for the state of wishing something undone. It occurs four times in the Quran, and here it is placed between the act and the punishment, with no gap on either side.
Literally to enter the morning, used in Arabic for coming into a state. It gives the regret a time of day: they did it, and by morning they were sorry.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Killing a camel was a public act with a known cost. A grown animal represented years of a family's wealth, and there were established payments for one destroyed. Hamstringing in particular was the way an animal was brought down for slaughter or out of spite, and it could not be done quietly or by accident. Everyone in an Arabian town would have known within the hour who had done it.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for what was done to the camel occurs three times in the Quran and every occurrence is about this one animal. The word for their regret occurs four times, and here it falls between the act and the punishment with nothing in between. Two ayat later a different people are named and the sequence begins again.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Remorse is separated from repentance, and the separation is the whole point. Feeling sorry is described as having occurred, promptly and genuinely, and it is not treated as a turning. What the Quran elsewhere calls turning back involves a change of direction, and there was no direction left to change once the animal was down. The passage does not say regret is worthless. It says regret is not the same thing as return.

crossReferences.why: Names the single man who did it, and describes what came after in one sentence.
Gives the same act in a short surah, with the whole people held to account for it.
Distinguishes turning back in time from regret expressed when nothing can follow it.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you regret and ask what turning would look like now, in an action rather than a feeling. A message, a repayment, a habit stopped this week. If there is nothing available, say so honestly and let the regret be regret. This passage separates the two, and confusing them is how people stay sorry for years without changing anything.

studies.title: What Your Lord Created For You
studies.meaning: Lot opens with the same four sentences every prophet in this sequence has used, and then puts his question. It is asked as a contrast rather than as an accusation: you approach the males among all creatures, and you leave what your Lord created for you in your wives. Then a single word closes it, describing them as a people who transgress. The account gives no scene and no description. It gives a question and a verdict, in two lines.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Lot's people are placed by the Quran in the towns south of the Dead Sea, on the road Meccan caravans travelled, and the previous surah referred to those ruins directly. The commentators note that this account, like the others in the sequence, is compressed to its exchange: the message, the question, the refusal, the outcome. No occasion is reported for these ayat, and the reasoning offered is about what was made rather than about a rule.

keyTerms.note: A plural of the word for male, occurring once in the Quran. Its pairing in the next line with the word for spouses sets the question up as one of two alternatives rather than as a list of acts.
The word for one of a pair, used throughout the Quran for husbands and wives alike. Describing them as created for you frames the alternative as a provision rather than as a requirement.
From the verb for crossing a boundary, the same root behind hostility and aggression. It occurs once in the Quran, and it names overstepping in general rather than any single act.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Lot's towns were a landmark on the Meccan trade road north, and the ruins were pointed out to travellers as a matter of course. The Quran refers to the site repeatedly and expects recognition rather than explanation, in the same way it refers to Aad and Thamud. For the first audience this was not a story from another civilisation. It was a place on the itinerary, described by men who had passed it.
studies.didYouKnow: Two of the words in these two lines occur once each in the whole Quran: the plural used for the males, and the word describing the people as those who overstep. Lot's account is among the shortest of the five in this sequence, and the four lines that open it are word for word the same as the four that open the other four.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument is put in terms of what was made rather than of what is decreed. Lot points at an arrangement already in place and asks why it is being set aside, which locates the reasoning in creation rather than in an announced rule. That is the pattern of this whole surah, where every prophet argues from something the listeners can already see. The verdict that closes it names a disposition, overstepping, rather than a single deed.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same question in slightly different words, with the same contrast between the two.
Repeats the account with the added detail that they acted knowingly.
Names the spouse relation as a sign, with tranquillity and affection placed between them.

studies.applyIt: Notice one thing you have been given and have stopped using: a skill, a relationship, an hour of the day that is actually free. Not a moral failing, just a provision going unspent. Pick one and use it once this week. Lot's question is about leaving aside what was made available, and the shape of that question reaches further than its occasion.

studies.title: Deliver Me And My Family
studies.meaning: The threat is expulsion, and the word is a definite plural: you will be among the driven out. Lot's answer separates the act from the people with unusual precision. He says he is one of those who detest your deed, naming the conduct and not the persons. Then he stops speaking to them and prays, and the prayer asks to be delivered from what they do rather than from them. The deliverance follows in one line, with one exception.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Expulsion was the sanction a town used on a man it could not silence, and the same threat was made to Noah earlier in this surah in the same grammatical form. The old woman left behind is identified in other surahs as Lot's wife, and the Quran states plainly that she stayed among those who remained. The commentators do not go further than the text does. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: A definite plural, occurring once in the Quran. It matches the form of the threat made to Noah in this same surah, where the word was those who are stoned, and that word is also used once.

A strong word for loathing, occurring once in the Quran. Lot attaches it to their deed rather than to them, and the Arabic makes the object explicit, so the sentence cannot be read as being about the persons.
A participle for remaining behind when others move on. It occurs seven times in the Quran, and every one of them names the same person, always without a further explanation of her choice.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A man driven out of his town in Arabia lost everything at once: the well he drew from, the protection that kept him alive, the market he traded in and the graves of his family. Exile was a practical death sentence with an interval. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and his community made exactly that journey out of Mecca, and the first audience for this passage included people who were living the threat.
studies.didYouKnow: Two of the words here occur once each in the Quran, and they are the threat and the answer to it: those who are driven out, and those who detest. The word for the one left behind occurs seven times across the Book, and every occurrence names the same person, and never with an explanation of it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The prayer is precise about what it asks to be saved from. Lot does not ask for their punishment or for his enemies to be handled; he asks to be delivered from what they do, which makes the danger a practice rather than a set of people. That distinction is held throughout: the word he uses for loathing is attached to the deed. And the exception at the end shows that proximity to a prophet secures nothing on its own.

crossReferences.why: Records the same deliverance and the same exception, with the reason given as a decree.
Names the wives of two prophets who were not saved by the households they were in.
Gives the night of the visitors at Lot's house and the instruction to leave before dawn.

studies.applyIt: Try Lot's grammar the next time you are angry with someone. Name the thing they did rather than what they are: this decision, not this person. It is a small change in a sentence and it is remarkably hard to make. Notice what it does to the conversation, and notice what it does to you while you are saying it.

studies.title: An Evil Kind Of Rain
studies.meaning: The destruction is named and then described with one image, and the image is a reversal. We rained on them a rain; and evil was the rain of those who had been warned. Rain in this book is the standard picture of mercy arriving from the sky, and here the same verb delivers the opposite. Nothing is said about what fell. Then the refrain, and then the last of the seven peoples is named, and this one is identified by a place rather than by descent.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The people named at the end are called the companions of the thicket, a wooded place the commentators locate near Midian in the north-west of the peninsula. The Quran names them four times. The commentators discuss whether they were the same community as the people of Midian or a neighbouring one, and preserve both readings without deciding. No occasion is reported for these ayat.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary verb for rainfall, used here of a destruction. The Quran keeps the word and changes the cargo, so the sentence has to be read twice before the reversal registers.
A passive participle, so the emphasis falls on their having received the warning rather than on their having refused it. The rain is described as belonging to them, which makes the outcome theirs.
A tangled stand of trees, unusual enough in Arabia to name a people by. The Quran mentions it four times, and this community is the only one in the sequence identified by its landscape.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Rain was the year's single most watched event. Men read cloud and wind for it, moved herds toward it, and a season without it emptied a settlement. The Quran uses rainfall for mercy constantly and the audience felt the metaphor as a fact. Turning the same verb into an instrument of ruin took a word that meant relief in every previous sentence and made it arrive as the opposite, which is a specific kind of shock.
studies.didYouKnow: The people named at the close of this passage are the only ones in the sequence not introduced as the brother of their audience. Every other prophet here is called their brother; this one is simply named. The commentators note the difference and connect it to the wording of the opening, which uses a place rather than a lineage to identify the community.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The same act delivers mercy and ruin depending on nothing visible in the act itself. Rain falls either way; what changes is what it carries and whom it reaches. That is a claim about how the world works under God rather than about weather: the ordinary machinery of life is not neutral, and its direction is not something a person can read off its surface. The refrain then closes on mercy, as it has after every ending.

crossReferences.why: Places the same ruined town on the road the Meccans travelled and names the same rain.
Gives the destruction of the same people in different imagery, with stones marked and sent.
Names the companions of the thicket immediately after Lot's people, as this passage does.

studies.applyIt: Think of something that arrived in your life looking like one thing and turned out to be the other, in either direction. A job that came at the wrong moment. An offer you were glad to take. Write one sentence about each. This passage puts mercy and ruin in the same verb, and the exercise is to sit with how little the surface told you.

studies.title: Give The Measure In Full
studies.meaning: Shu'ayb is introduced without the word that introduced the four before him. Every other prophet in this run was called their brother; he is named alone. Then the template runs exactly as before, four sentences unchanged, and the fifth breaks into something no other prophet in the sequence asks for. Fill the measure, and do not be among those who cause loss. The demand is commercial, and it is put in the same breath as wariness of God.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The people of the thicket lay on the trade road between Arabia and Syria, and the commentators describe them as a merchant community whose living came from goods passing through. Mecca was the same kind of place. Every listener there handled a measure or a balance in the course of a week, and short measure was the specific dishonesty a trading town could not police. No occasion is reported for these ayat.

keyTerms.note: The measure is a container of fixed volume used for grain and dates. Filling it up means to the brim, so the instruction is about the last handful rather than about the general practice.
From the verb for making someone lose out. It occurs once in the Quran, and it names the effect on the other party rather than the gain to the one measuring.
The word appears in the same sentence four other prophets used, but it lands differently here, because the instruction that follows is about whether a man can be trusted with a measure.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca lived on caravans, and a caravan settled up by measure and weight at both ends. A merchant filled a container for the buyer and had one filled for him by the supplier, and the difference between honest and shaved measure over a season was a real income. There were no inspectors. The whole system ran on whether a man could be trusted when nobody was counting, which is why this instruction is the one Shu'ayb leads with.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for those who cause loss occurs once in the whole Quran, here. And Shu'ayb is the one prophet in this sequence of five who is not introduced as the people's brother; the other four all are, in the identical phrase. The commentators connect the difference to the way this community is named, by its place rather than by its ancestry.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The sequence has run four times with the same opening and no specific content after it. Here the content arrives, and it is a trading instruction. That places honest measure in the position the other accounts gave to idols and to excess, which says something about where this community's actual refusal lived. Wariness of God and filling a container to the brim are put in consecutive sentences, and the passage does not treat the second as a lesser matter.

crossReferences.why: Describes exactly this practice, taking full measure from others and giving short in return.
Gives Shu'ayb's message to Midian, opening with the same instruction about measure and balance.
States the same instruction and calls the outcome better and finer in the end.

studies.applyIt: Look for the place in your week where you give slightly less than the full amount and nobody would notice. The last ten minutes of a shift, the reply you shortened, the corner cut on something you were paid for. Give the full measure once, deliberately, in that exact place. Nobody will remark on it, which is the point of the instruction.

studies.title: Weigh With A True Balance
studies.meaning: The instructions continue and widen. Weigh with the straight balance; do not shortchange people in their things; do not go about the earth spreading ruin. Then a turn back to God, described as the one who created you and the generations before. Their answer contains no reference to any of it. You are bewitched; you are only a human being like us; and we think you are lying. Three dismissals, none of them about measure.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The word used for the balance is a loanword the classical lexicographers traced outside Arabic, which suits a passage about the instruments of international trade. The commentators note that the three answers Shu'ayb receives are the same three the Quraysh were giving in Mecca: possession, ordinariness and lying. The sequence is preserved as a set rather than argued with. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: A beam balance with two pans. The classical lexicographers treat the word as taken into Arabic from outside it, and it occurs twice in the Quran, both times in an instruction about weighing.
To reduce what is owed to somebody, whether in goods, price or credit. The verb occurs three times in the Quran, and all three are in passages where Shu'ayb is speaking.
A rare word for created masses of people. It reaches past the listeners' own ancestors to everyone made before them, which places the demand for honest dealing inside the whole history of being made.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A balance was two pans on a beam with a set of stone or metal weights, and everyone knew that a weight could be shaved, a pan could be weighted underneath and a beam could be set slightly off centre. Disputes over weight were common and hard to settle, since proving the fraud meant proving what the instrument had done in someone else's hand. Trust in the tool was trust in the man holding it.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for shortchanging people occurs three times in the Quran, and every occurrence is Shu'ayb speaking, in three different surahs. The word for the balance appears twice, and the classical lexicographers already regarded it as a term borrowed into Arabic, which fits a vocabulary that travelled with the goods it was used to weigh.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Fair dealing is grounded in creation rather than in contract. Shu'ayb finishes a list of trading instructions by naming the one who made both the listeners and everyone before them, which puts the scales inside a relationship rather than inside a market. The reply is worth noticing too: nothing in it addresses the instruction. When a demand is inconvenient, the fastest route is to attack the person who made it, and all three answers do that.

crossReferences.why: Places the balance in the heavens and tells people not to fall short in it.
Gives the same instructions to Midian, with the same warning about shortchanging people.
Asks whether those who do it consider that they will be raised for a great day.

studies.applyIt: Check one number you report on that nobody audits. Hours logged, a mileage claim, the figure you round when someone asks how much. Make it exact once this week, even at your own cost, and notice how small the cost actually is. Shu'ayb's instruction is about the last handful in the container, and so is this.

studies.title: My Lord Knows What You Do
studies.meaning: They ask to be destroyed. Drop pieces of the sky on us, if you are truthful, which turns the demand for a sign into a dare. Shu'ayb's answer is four words and it does not accept the terms: my Lord knows best what you do. He neither calls the punishment down nor argues that it will come. The next sentence gives the outcome anyway, and it names the day by an image nobody explains: the day of the canopy.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The day named at the end occurs once in the Quran and is left undescribed; the commentators report that a cloud gathered which the people took for shade and which brought the punishment, and they record it as a report rather than as something the text states. The Quraysh made the same dare in Mecca, asking for pieces of the sky to be dropped on them. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: Broken sections of something, used of the sky in several places. The demand is for the roof of the world to come apart in chunks, which is the most extreme sign a person could name.
A comparative form, so the answer is not that God knows but that He knows better than the speaker does. Shu'ayb hands the assessment over instead of making one.
A covering that casts shade, from the ordinary word for shadow. It occurs once in the Quran, naming a day by the thing that looked like relief before it turned out to be the punishment.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Shade in that climate was the first thing anyone looked for. A cloud crossing the sun in the middle of the day was a relief people stopped to enjoy, and a large one drew a whole settlement out to stand under it. That is what makes the name of the day work on an Arabian audience without a word of explanation. The thing they walked toward was the thing that took them.
studies.didYouKnow: The word naming the day of this punishment occurs once in the Quran, and it means a canopy of shade. The Quran gives no further description of what happened. The Quraysh in Mecca made the same demand recorded here, asking for the sky to be brought down on them in pieces, and the Quran preserves both versions of the dare in nearly the same words.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Shu'ayb is handed the role of judge and refuses it. He could have said the punishment is coming, or that they deserve it, and he says only that God knows what they are doing. That leaves the assessment where it belongs and keeps the messenger from becoming the one who decides. The naming of the day afterwards is not his doing and is not addressed to them, which preserves the separation the answer established.

crossReferences.why: Records the Meccans making the same demand, that the sky be dropped on them in pieces.
Preserves another version of the dare, asking for stones from the sky if this is the truth.
Gives the same confrontation with Midian and the outcome that followed it.

studies.applyIt: When somebody dares you to prove them wrong, notice that the dare has already set the terms. You do not have to accept them. Try Shu'ayb's answer in your own words: I do not know, and it is not mine to settle. It sounds weak and it ends more arguments than winning does, because there is nothing left to push against.

studies.title: Brought Down Upon Your Heart
studies.meaning: The seven accounts end and the surah turns to its own text. It is a sending down from the Lord of the worlds; the trustworthy Spirit came down with it; upon your heart, so that you would be one of the warners; in a clear Arabic tongue. Four short lines that name a source, a carrier, a destination and a language. The destination is the striking one. Not upon your ears or your tongue. Upon your heart.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has spent nearly two hundred ayat on other prophets and now states, in four lines, what the recitation being heard actually is. The trustworthy Spirit is identified by the classical commentators as Gabriel. The claim that it came in clear Arabic answers a charge recorded elsewhere, that a foreigner was teaching him. No occasion is reported for these ayat, and the description is given without argument.

keyTerms.note: This exact phrase occurs once in the Quran. The second word is the same one five prophets in this surah used of themselves, so the carrier and the messengers are described as trustworthy in identical terms.
The heart in Quranic usage is the seat of understanding rather than of feeling. Naming it as the place of arrival makes revelation a matter of comprehension rather than of dictation to the ear.
Tongue here means language, as it does in English. The adjective that follows makes clarity part of the claim, so the language is described as doing work rather than as merely being the one used.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabic in that world was a spoken art before it was a written one. Poetry was composed in the head, carried by memory and judged by ear at the fairs, and a man's standing could rest on a few lines everyone could recite. A text that arrived in that language, in that register, was not entering a vacuum. It was entering a competition the audience already knew how to judge.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase naming the trustworthy Spirit occurs once in the whole Quran. Its second word is the one five prophets in this surah have already used to describe themselves, so the description of the carrier repeats, exactly, the claim each of them made. The Quran does not remark on the echo, and the surah simply moves on.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation is described as a route with four points, and every one of them is specified. That leaves no room for the message to be a product of the receiver, since the source, the carrier and the destination are all named separately. But the destination named is a heart, not a page or a mouth, which means the text was understood before it was spoken. Language is placed last, as the form the understanding took.

crossReferences.why: Names Gabriel as the one who brought it down upon the heart, by God's permission.
Answers the charge that a foreigner taught him, by naming the language as clear Arabic.
Describes the same sending of a spirit, and what the recipient had not known before.

studies.applyIt: Read a short passage of the Quran today and stop after it, without moving to the next thing for one minute. No commentary, no phone. This passage says the text arrived at a heart before it arrived at a tongue, and reading it back the same way, understanding before recitation, takes a minute you can find today.

studies.title: The Scholars Already Knew It
studies.meaning: Two claims and a thought experiment. It is in the scriptures of the earlier peoples; and is it not a sign for them that the learned among the Children of Israel recognise it? Then the experiment: if this had been sent down on one of the non-Arabs and he had recited it to them, they would not have believed. The point is not about language. It is that a reason to refuse was always going to be available.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Jewish and Christian communities lived across the peninsula and their learned men were consulted on matters of scripture, including by the Quraysh. The Quran appeals to that recognition without naming individuals. Later reports identify particular figures, and those reports vary and are not part of the Quranic statement. The thought experiment answers an objection about the messenger being one of their own. No occasion is attested for these ayat.

keyTerms.note: A plural for written records, used in the Quran for revealed books given before. The word points at texts rather than at oral tradition, which is what makes the claim checkable in principle.
Those with knowledge, used here of a group outside the immediate audience. The argument appeals to expertise held by people who had no reason to support the claim, which is why the appeal has force.

From a root for speech that is unclear to the listener, so the word names foreignness by language rather than by origin. It occurs once in the Quran, inside a sentence that is imagining rather than describing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The Quraysh did send to learned men outside Mecca when they wanted a question about scripture settled, and the reports describe them travelling for answers about what a prophet should be able to tell them. Jewish communities were established in Yathrib and in the oases to the north, and Christian ones in the south and along the trade routes. Consulting them was a normal step, not an unusual one.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for non-Arabic speakers occurs once in the whole Quran, and it appears inside a hypothetical rather than a description. The argument it belongs to is unusual for scripture: it imagines a version of itself that did not happen and states what the outcome would have been, which concedes that the language was never the actual objection.
studies.theologicalSignificance: An objection is answered by removing it and showing that nothing changes. The passage does not argue that Arabic was necessary; it grants the alternative and says the refusal would have stood anyway. That relocates unbelief from the properties of the message to a decision in the listener, which is the same point the surah has been making through seven accounts. The appeal to outside scholars adds evidence, without making the case depend on it.

crossReferences.why: Describes people given knowledge before who fall down when it is recited to them.
Puts the same hypothetical, asking what would be said if the recitation were foreign.
States that those given the Book before know it was sent down with the truth.

studies.applyIt: Notice the reason you give for not doing something, and ask what you would say if that reason were removed. Not enough time, then time appears. Too expensive, then it is free. If a second reason arrives instantly, the first one was never the obstacle. This passage runs that test on an objection, and it is worth running on your own.

studies.title: It Passes Through Their Hearts
studies.meaning: The verb is one of threading something through a narrow place, and the object is the message and the place is their hearts. It goes in, and it does not stop there. What follows describes the condition precisely: they will not believe until they see the punishment, and by then it arrives suddenly, with no notice, and their first words are a request for delay. The passage ends by turning their own impatience back on them as a question.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quraysh had asked more than once for the promised punishment to be brought forward, treating the delay as proof that nothing was coming. The commentators read the closing question as answering that demand directly. The form of the verb in the first line is unusual and occurs only here, and the commentators discuss whether the message passes into the heart without being received or passes through it. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: From a verb for passing something through a narrow opening, like a thread through a needle or a road through a pass. This form occurs once in the Quran, and it makes the message something inserted rather than offered.
An adverb for something arriving with no approach. The Quran uses it thirteen times, almost always of an appointed thing whose date was known to be coming and whose hour was not.
From the verb for waiting and looking. It names being given more time, and it occurs in this form once in the Quran, in a question asked by people who had asked for less time.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Delay was the standard mercy in Arabian dealings. A debt could be deferred, a blood feud suspended for the sacred months, a judgement postponed while an intermediary worked. Everyone knew how to ask for more time and what it cost to grant it. The people in this passage had spent years treating the absence of a punishment as its non-existence, and then asked for exactly the thing they had been given all along.
studies.didYouKnow: Two words in this short passage occur once each in the Quran: the verb for threading the message through their hearts, and the participle they use to ask whether they will be given more time. The second sits one line before a question about them wanting the punishment hastened, and the surah puts the two requests next to each other without comment.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Belief that waits for proof is described as arriving too late by definition. The condition named is not that they cannot believe but that they will not until the evidence is the punishment itself, at which point belief is no longer a response to anything. And the last line exposes the incoherence gently: the people asking for the thing to be brought forward are the same ones who will ask for it to be held back. The two requests are the same misunderstanding.

crossReferences.why: Shows belief arriving at the moment of drowning, and being refused for that reason.
Answers the same demand to hasten the punishment, and says the decision is not the messenger's.
Describes faith declared when the punishment is seen, and says it did not benefit them.

studies.applyIt: Notice one thing you are waiting for proof about before you act. The scan result before you change how you eat. The argument settled before you apologise. There may be good reasons. But ask whether the proof you are waiting for is the kind that arrives only after the decision has been made for you, and act accordingly.

studies.title: Years That Availed Them Nothing
studies.meaning: A hypothesis is put and then collapsed. Suppose We let them enjoy themselves for years, and then what was promised comes. What would the enjoyment have done for them? The question is not answered because it does not need to be. Then a statement about the whole record of destroyed towns: none was ended without warners sent to it first, as a reminder. And a final clause that is doing the real work. We were not unjust.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has just told seven accounts, each one a town that received a warner and refused him, so the claim here is a summary of what the reader has been shown rather than an assertion arriving from nowhere. The commentators note the placement: the general principle is stated only after the cases. The final clause answers an objection nobody in the text has raised. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: An intensive verb for giving someone the use of something for a period. The word carries a term built into it, so what is granted is enjoyment with an end date attached from the start.
Standing alone as a single word, without a verb, which is unusual. It names the purpose of the warners in one term: not a threat and not a condition, but something placed so a person could remember.
From a root for putting a thing where it does not belong, and by extension for darkness. Applied here in a denial about God, it closes the sequence on a claim about fairness rather than about power.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Warning was a formal act in Arabian society. A man who intended to attack a settlement sent notice first, and raiding without it was held against him afterwards; a creditor gave notice before seizing property. Acting without warning was the mark of a man with no honour. Saying that no town was ended without warners first is therefore a claim in a legal register the audience recognised immediately.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the reminder stands on its own in the middle of this passage, a single noun with no verb attached, which the classical grammarians discuss at some length. And the clause that closes it is a denial rather than an assertion: not that God is just, but that He was not unjust. The surah's whole sequence of seven towns is the evidence for it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage puts a procedural guarantee where a reader expects a threat. Nobody is ended without notice, and the notice is described as a reminder rather than as a condition met or failed. That makes the warnings themselves part of the mercy rather than part of the sentence. And the denial at the end places God under a standard the reader can check, which is why the seven accounts had to come first. The claim is offered with its evidence attached.

crossReferences.why: States that no community was left without a warner passing through it.
Says no people are punished until a messenger has been sent to them.
Gives the same collapse of a long enjoyment into a morning's worth of dry grass.

studies.applyIt: Give somebody a warning you have been meaning to give and have kept putting off. Not a threat, a notice: I am going to stop covering this, the deadline is real, I am worried about you. One conversation, this week. The passage makes advance notice a matter of fairness, and most of the unfairness in ordinary life is silence that arrives too late.

studies.title: Warn Your Nearest Kin
studies.meaning: A charge is answered in three short lines. The satans did not bring this down; it would not suit them; and they could not, because they are cut off from the hearing. Then the address turns, without transition, to the one receiving it. Do not call on another god beside God. And warn your closest relatives. The sequence is deliberate: after two hundred ayat about distant peoples, the instruction is about the people in the next room.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The command to warn the nearest kin is one of the best attested in the classical sources, which describe the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) climbing a hill in Mecca, calling the clans by name and asking whether they would believe him if he told them an army was on the far side. His own uncle answered him. The occasion is reported with unusual consistency, and the commentators treat it as established.

keyTerms.note: A passive participle for being set aside from something. It occurs once in the Quran, and the passive matters: they are not merely unable, they have been removed from the position.

The circle of relatives a man belongs to by blood, wider than a household and narrower than a tribe. The word occurs once in the Quran in this form, and it is the audience named for the first warning.
A verb for what suits or befits a thing. The denial says the task does not belong to their nature before it says they lack the power, so unsuitability is given as a reason in its own right.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Warning your own clan first was how any serious news moved in Mecca. A man who had learned of a danger told his kin before the town, because they were the people he owed and the people who would act on his word. It was also the hardest audience. They knew him as a child, they had a claim on him, and they could refuse him in a way strangers could not, in front of everyone who mattered.
studies.didYouKnow: Two words in this passage occur once each in the Quran: the participle saying the satans are barred from listening, and the word for the nearest kin who are to be warned. They sit four lines apart, and the surah moves from a claim about who could not have brought the message to an instruction about who should hear it first.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The denial is made on three grounds and only one of them is about capability. It would not suit them, and they are barred, and they could not: motive, access and power, each closed separately. Then the instruction that follows narrows the whole surah to a doorstep. Seven peoples across centuries have been described, and what is asked for is a conversation with the relatives who will find it hardest to take the speaker seriously.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same barring, with those who used to sit and listen finding the way guarded.
Records Abraham's care for a close relative, and where that care reached its limit.
Places responsibility for a household on the person inside it, in the same direction.

studies.applyIt: Say the one true thing you have been avoiding saying to a family member. Not the whole conversation. One sentence, said once, without a follow-up campaign. This is the hardest audience there is, which is exactly why the instruction names them, and the difficulty is not a sign that you have chosen wrongly.

studies.title: Lower Your Wing To Them
studies.meaning: Four instructions in four lines, and the first is an image. Lower your wing to the believers who follow you, which is what a bird does over its young, and the same phrase is used elsewhere of a person's conduct toward ageing parents. If they disobey you, say you are clear of what they do, and nothing further. Then rely on the Mighty, the Merciful, the pair of names that has closed every account in this surah.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan.
