The instruction arrives immediately after the command to warn the nearest kin, so it concerns the community that had begun to form around a man whose relatives were refusing him. The last two lines describe God seeing him when he stands and as he moves among those who prostrate, which the commentators read as covering both his prayer alone and his prayer with others. No occasion is reported for these ayat.

keyTerms.note: A bird settling its wing over what it shelters. The instruction occurs three times in the Quran, once toward parents, and it names a posture of gentleness rather than an act.
From a root for being healed or released from a liability, used in trade for a debt discharged. It is a statement about responsibility rather than about affection, and it does not sever the relation.
A noun for turning over and shifting position. It occurs once in the Quran, and it describes being seen not in a single posture but through the whole sequence of movements a person makes.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Leadership in Arabia was assertive by default. A chief held position by presence, by the ability to hold a room and to be answered, and softness toward followers read as weakness that invited challenge. The instruction here runs against that, and it is given to a man whose community was small, poor and under pressure, at exactly the moment when a leader in that world would have been expected to tighten his grip.
studies.didYouKnow: The instruction to lower the wing occurs three times in the Quran. One of them is about parents, where it is joined to mercy and to a prayer for them; another is addressed to a prophet about his followers, as here. The word for the moving about that God is said to see occurs once in the whole Book.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Authority is given and then immediately softened. The man told to warn his relatives is told in the next breath to be gentle with the people who came, and to say only that he is clear of their conduct if they will not follow. No enforcement is provided and none is implied. What is provided instead is the assurance that he is seen: standing, and moving among those who prostrate, which places the observer inside the congregation rather than above it.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same image of the lowered wing, there for the treatment of ageing parents.
Gives the same instruction to lower the wing to the believers, alongside a warning against envy.
Says that harshness would have driven people away from around him, and tells him to pardon them.

studies.applyIt: Choose one person who follows your lead, at work or at home, and be visibly gentler with them this week than the situation requires. Not lenient about the task. Gentle in the manner: how you ask, how you correct, how long you let them finish a sentence. The instruction here is about posture, and posture is something other people can feel.

studies.title: Upon Whom The Devils Descend
studies.meaning: The question is put as an offer of information. Shall I tell you on whom the satans do come down? They come down on every habitual liar, deep in wrongdoing; such people strain to catch something, and most of what they pass on is false. Then the sentence that gives the surah its name. And the poets, the wayward follow them. Nothing about verse is said yet. What is described first is an audience.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quraysh had accounted for the recitation by calling it the work of a poet or of a soothsayer with an unseen informant, and these lines answer both at once. Poetry in that society was a form of power, used to praise, to shame and to fight, and poets were kept by tribes for the purpose. The surah takes its name from this ayah. No occasion is reported for the passage.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form, so not one who lied but one who does it as a practice. It occurs twice in the Quran, and it names a disposition rather than an occasion.
Literally to cast the hearing toward something, the way a person strains to catch a conversation. The verb is the same one used five times earlier in this surah for throwing a staff or a rope.
Those who have wandered off a path deliberately rather than by mistake. The passage puts them as the followers rather than as the poets, so the criticism starts with who is listening.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A tribal poet was a weapon. His verses were memorised, carried by travellers and recited at the fairs, and a satire could damage a clan's marriage prospects and its trade for a generation. Tribes paid poets, protected them and feared the ones on the other side. Being told that a message was poetry was therefore not a comment on its style. It was a claim about what it was for.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for straining to overhear is the same one the surah used five times in the contest with the magicians, for casting a staff, casting ropes and being cast down. Its last appearance in the surah is this one, and what is thrown is an ear. The word for the habitual liar occurs twice in the Quran.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The test offered is about character rather than about content. Instead of arguing over whether the words are inspired, the passage describes who receives that kind of communication: someone who lies as a habit and does wrong as a practice. That makes the messenger's known life the evidence, which is a check anybody in Mecca could run. And when the poets are named, the sentence describes their following first, which puts the audience inside the diagnosis.

crossReferences.why: Denies that the recitation is the speech of a poet or of a soothsayer.
States that poetry was not taught to him and would not be fitting for him.
Describes the guarding of the heavens against those who used to sit and listen.

studies.applyIt: Check the character of one source before you check its claims. Not whether you agree, whether the person tells the truth when it costs them something. It is slower than fact-checking and it works on things you cannot verify. This passage offers that test in place of an argument, and it was offered to people who had known the speaker all his life.

studies.title: Except Those Who Remember Much
studies.meaning: Two charges and then an exception that reopens everything. They wander in every valley; they say what they do not do. Both are about the gap between speech and life. Then the last ayah of the surah takes four qualities and lifts a whole class out of the verdict: those who believed, did good, remembered God much, and defended themselves after being wronged. Poetry is not condemned. What is condemned is saying what you are not.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The exception is reported by the commentators as covering the poets who joined the community and used verse in its defence, and the classical sources describe the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) receiving such verse and approving of it. The surah ends here, at ayah two hundred and twenty-seven, and it is the second longest surah in the Quran by number of ayat. No further occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: Used of a camel roaming without direction, and of a man distracted by love. It occurs once in the Quran, and it describes movement with no destination rather than movement in the wrong one.
A reflexive form of the verb for being helped, so the sense is taking one's own part. It is placed after being wronged, which keeps the defence a response rather than an initiative.

keyTerms.gloss: an overturning, a place of return
keyTerms.note: From the verb for turning something over. It occurs once in the Quran, and the sentence uses the noun and the verb together, so the closing line turns on the same word twice.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A poet's licence in Arabia was total. He could praise a patron beyond truth, satirise an enemy beyond decency, and boast of deeds nobody had seen, and the audience judged the craft rather than the claim. Verse was expected to exaggerate. Naming that gap between what a man says and what he does was therefore not a criticism of bad poetry. It was a criticism of the whole arrangement.
studies.didYouKnow: Two words in the last three ayat of this surah occur once each in the Quran: the verb for wandering in every valley, and the noun for the overturning at the very end. The final sentence pairs that noun with its own verb, so the Book's second longest surah closes on a word turned back on itself.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The exception is what makes the passage usable. A whole profession is described in two lines and then a door is left open, and the door is not narrow: belief, good work, remembrance and self-defence after wrong. Nothing about the craft itself has to change. What has to close is the distance between what is said and what is done, which is a standard the reader shares with the poets rather than one applied only to them.

crossReferences.why: States plainly how hateful it is to say what you do not do, in the same terms.
Names remembering God much as an instruction in its own right, as the exception here does.
Places self-defence after wrong beside pardon, and describes what each of them costs.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you have said about yourself out loud this month and have not done. Then either do the smallest version of it today or stop saying it. That is the whole choice this passage offers, and the surah ends by leaving the door open rather than by closing it. Which of the two you take is less important than making it deliberate.
